papers.core_contribution: Provides a unified theoretical perspective on implicit neural representations (INRs), showing they are analogous to structured signal dictionaries with harmonics, and that their inductive bias is characterized by the neural tangent kernel (NTK), with meta-learning reshaping the NTK like dictionary learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzes the expressive power and inductive bias of INRs from a unified perspective, showing harmonic expansion and NTK characterization, and reveals that meta-learning modifies the NTK to increase efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
INRs have expressive power equivalent to structured signal dictionaries whose atoms are integer harmonics of the input mapping frequencies.
The frequency support of INRs grows exponentially with depth as each layer splits input into higher order harmonics.
INRs suffer from failure modes such as imperfect recovery and aliasing due to their harmonic expansion.
The inductive bias of INRs is captured by the ability of their empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) to encode target signals efficiently.
Meta-learning increases the encoding efficiency of the NTK by constructing a rich signal dictionary from combinations of meta-training tasks.
papers.limitation: Most practical results are performed using one or two-dimensional signals, and insights should be extensible to higher dimensions.
future_direction: Generalize Theorem 1 to input mappings beyond sinusoids or include normalization layers.
Study the effect of out-of-distribution data on the alignment with the NTK after meta-training.
Design methods to visualize the eigenfunctions of the NTK in higher dimensions.
papers.abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to classical discretized representations of signals. Nevertheless, despite their practical success, we still do not understand how INRs represent signals. We propose a novel unified perspective to theoretically analyse INRs. Leveraging results from harmonic analysis and deep learning theory, we show that most INR families are analogous to structured signal dictionaries whose atoms are integer harmonics of the set of initial mapping frequencies. This structure allows INRs to express signals with an exponentially increasing frequency support using a number of parameters that only grows linearly with depth. We also explore the inductive bias of INRs exploiting recent results about the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK). Specifically, we show that the eigenfunctions of the NTK can be seen as dictionary atoms whose inner product with the target signal determines the final performance of their reconstruction. In this regard, we reveal that meta-learning has a reshaping effect on the NTK analogous to dictionary learning, building dictionary atoms as a combination of the examples seen during meta-training. Our results permit to design and tune novel INR architectures, but can also be of interest for the wider deep learning theory community.

papers.title: Causal Convolutional Neural Networks as Finite Impulse Response Filters
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether Causal Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with quasi-linear activation functions, when applied to time-series data with multimodal frequency content, exhibit properties analogous to Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters and can be reduced to an equivalent single-layer filter.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Causal CNNs with quasi-linear activations and long convolutional kernels behave like FIR filters, and the entire network can be reduced to an equivalent single-layer FIR filter optimized via least-squares, providing interpretability for system identification tasks.
papers.conclusion: Causal CNNs with quasi-linear activations and long kernels can be interpreted as FIR filters, offering a bridge between black-box neural networks and physically interpretable models for system identification in structural dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Causal CNNs with long kernels and quasi-linear activations can approximate band-pass FIR filters when trained on spectrally sparse data.
A multi-layer CCNN can be combined into a single equivalent FIR filter that is optimal in the least-squares sense, whereas a single-layer CCNN fails to achieve comparable performance.
In supervised regression, the learned CCNN filters implicitly capture the modal properties (natural frequencies) of a multi-degree-of-freedom dynamical system.
In an unsupervised setting using a VAE with a CCNN decoder, the model can learn and separate the natural modes of the system without access to excitation data.
The method is validated on real-world bridge vibration data (Z24 benchmark), showing recovery of expected natural frequencies.
papers.limitation:
The tanh-activated CNN is effectively linear only when activations lie predominantly near zero, which is a condition for interpretability as an FIR filter.
In the unsupervised learning task on a 9-DOF system, only the first 4 natural modes were reliably recovered, as higher modes were suppressed in the raw system dynamics.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the behavior of Causal Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with quasi-linear activation functions when applied to time-series data characterized by multimodal frequency content. We demonstrate that, once trained, such networks exhibit properties analogous to Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters, particularly when the convolutional kernels are of extended length exceeding those typically employed in standard CNN architectures. Causal CNNs are shown to capture spectral features both implicitly and explicitly, offering enhanced interpretability for tasks involving dynamic systems. Leveraging the associative property of convolution, we further show that the entire network can be reduced to an equivalent single-layer filter resembling an FIR filter optimized via least-squares criteria. This equivalence yields new insights into the spectral learning behavior of CNNs trained on signals with sparse frequency content. The approach is validated on both simulated beam dynamics and real-world bridge vibration datasets, underlining its relevance for modeling and identifying physical systems governed by dynamic responses.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Mechanistic Neural Networks for Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks that explicitly learn and solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) as representations in a parallel and scalable way to enhance interpretability and efficiency in scientific machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Mechanistic Neural Networks, a novel neural network design that incorporates a Mechanistic Block to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, and a parallel, differentiable ODE solver (NeuRLP) for efficient and scalable training in scientific machine learning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic Neural Networks are a powerful and versatile approach for scientific machine learning, capable of discovering and modeling complex dynamical systems with high interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic Neural Networks can discover governing equations from data and outperform the SINDy method in some cases, including for nonlinear and rational function derivatives.
The NeuRLP solver is efficient, parallel, and allows for faster training and longer rollouts compared to traditional sequential ODE solvers like Runge-Kutta.
The method is versatile and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on a range of scientific ML tasks, including PDE solving, equation discovery, and dynamical systems modeling.
The NeuRLP solver can learn adaptive time steps, becoming finer in regions where the fit is poor.
The method can handle multiple independent trajectories and learn a single governing equation from them, improving generalization.
papers.limitation: The cumulative error of the NeuRLP solver can become large for equations where the coefficients c0/c2 and c1/c2 are large relative to the step size.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Mechanistic Neural Networks, a neural network design for machine learning applications in the sciences. It incorporates a new Mechanistic Block in standard architectures to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, revealing the underlying dynamics of data and enhancing interpretability and efficiency in data modeling. Central to our approach is a novel Relaxed Linear Programming Solver (NeuRLP) inspired by a technique that reduces solving linear ODEs to solving linear programs. This integrates well with neural networks and surpasses the limitations of traditional ODE solvers enabling scalable GPU parallel processing. Overall, Mechanistic Neural Networks demonstrate their versatility for scientific machine learning applications, adeptly managing tasks from equation discovery to dynamic systems modeling. We prove their comprehensive capabilities in analyzing and interpreting complex scientific data across various applications, showing significant performance against specialized state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Moirai-MoE: Empowering Time Series Foundation Models with Sparse Mixture of Experts
papers.research_question: How can time series foundation models achieve effective unified training by moving from human-imposed frequency-level specialization to automatic token-level specialization using sparse mixture of experts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MOIRAI-MOE, a time series foundation model that uses a single input/output projection layer and delegates pattern modeling to sparse mixture of experts, enabling automatic token-level specialization and improving forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: MOIRAI-MOE is an effective approach for time series foundation models, achieving token-level specialization and superior performance in forecasting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
MOIRAI-MOE outperforms existing foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) in both in-distribution and zero-shot forecasting.
The decoder-only training objective is more efficient than the masked encoder approach.
The proposed token clustering gating function outperforms linear projection gating variants.
Model analysis shows that MOIRAI-MOE produces frequency-invariant representations in deeper layers.
Expert allocation reflects time series periodicity patterns, indicating token-level specialization.
future_direction: Pruning underutilized experts for model compression
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models have demonstrated impressive performance as zero-shot forecasters. However, achieving effectively unified training on time series remains an open challenge. Existing approaches introduce some level of model specialization to account for the highly heterogeneous nature of time series data. For instance, Moirai pursues unified training by employing multiple input/output projection layers, each tailored to handle time series at a specific frequency. Similarly, TimesFM maintains a frequency embedding dictionary for this purpose. We identify two major drawbacks to this human-imposed frequency-level model specialization: (1) Frequency is not a reliable indicator of the underlying patterns in time series. For example, time series with different frequencies can display similar patterns, while those with the same frequency may exhibit varied patterns. (2) Non-stationarity is an inherent property of real-world time series, leading to varied distributions even within a short context window of a single time series. Frequency-level specialization is too coarse-grained to capture this level of diversity. To address these limitations, this paper introduces Moirai-MoE, using a single input/output projection layer while delegating the modeling of diverse time series patterns to the sparse mixture of experts (MoE) within Transformers. With these designs, Moirai-MoE reduces reliance on human-defined heuristics and enables automatic token-level specialization. Extensive experiments on 39 datasets demonstrate the superiority of Moirai-MoE over existing foundation models in both in-distribution and zero-shot scenarios. Furthermore, this study conducts comprehensive model analyses to explore the inner workings of time series MoE foundation models and provides valuable insights for future research.

papers.title: From Compass and Ruler to Convolution and Nonlinearity: On the Surprising Difficulty of Understanding a Simple CNN Solving a Simple Geometric Estimation Task
papers.research_question: What does a simple CNN learn when trained to estimate the radius of a centred pulse or disk, and why is understanding this surprisingly difficult?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the difficulty of understanding even simple CNNs and provides a full theoretical design of weights for a radius estimation task, highlighting the roles of invariance and nonlinear activation functions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals that invariance and the number of flat regions in activation functions are key concepts for understanding neural network expressiveness, providing insights for interpreting more complex models.
papers.key_findings:
A simple CNN with ReLU can estimate radius for positive polarity signals but fails for both polarities due to limited expressiveness.
Theoretical analysis allows designing all CNN weights, which match empirically learned weights.
Invariance to intensity differences is essential for correct estimation.
The shape of activation functions (e.g., number of plateaus) affects network expressiveness; Sigmoid with more plateaus can handle both polarities.
Adding more layers or channels can improve expressiveness but complicates analysis.
papers.limitation:
The network is underparametrised and not representative of complex real-world models.
The analysis assumes ideal conditions like clean data and continuum approximation.
future_direction: Investigating the impact of domain discretisation and radius quantisation.
Scaling the analysis to more complex problems and architectures.
Exploring the role of activation functions with more plateaus.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are omnipresent, but remain poorly understood. Their increasing complexity and use in critical systems raises the important challenge to full interpretability. We propose to address a simple well-posed learning problem: estimating the radius of a centred pulse in a one-dimensional signal or of a centred disk in two-dimensional images using a simple convolutional neural network. Surprisingly, understanding what trained networks have learned is difficult and, to some extent, counter-intuitive. However, an in-depth theoretical analysis in the one-dimensional case allows us to comprehend constraints due to the chosen architecture, the role of each filter and of the nonlinear activation function, and every single value taken by the weights of the model. Two fundamental concepts of neural networks arise: the importance of invariance and of the shape of the nonlinear activation functions.

papers.title: Local vs distributed representations: What is the right basis for interpretability?
papers.research_question: Are dictionary-based representations more interpretable than neuron-based representations for understanding convolutional neural networks, and how does the choice of representational basis affect model comparisons?
papers.core_contribution: Dictionary-based representations are consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations in CNNs, and model comparisons based solely on neuron-level analyses can be misleading due to differences in superposition.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary-based representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, and comparing models using only neuron-based representations can lead to misleading conclusions about their relative interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary-based representations were consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations across three psychophysics experiments, with the advantage increasing in deeper layers.
ResNet50 exhibits greater superposition (lower axis-alignment) than VGG16, which masks its higher interpretability in neuron-based comparisons.
ResNet50 is more interpretable than VGG16 when evaluated using dictionary-based representations, but this difference disappears when using neuron-based representations.
Dictionary elements are at least as decision-relevant as individual neurons, as measured by Gradient×Input importance.
papers.limitation:
The experimental protocol may be confounded by semantics, as participants could solve trials by simple semantic grouping rather than identifying visual patterns.
The study is limited to two CNN architectures (ResNet50 and VGG16).
future_direction: Further refinement of the experimental protocol to better mitigate semantic confounds.
Examination of the interpretability of dictionary elements recovered by applying dictionary learning to full layer activations.
Expanding the range of architectures to understand why certain models are inherently more interpretable than others.
papers.abstract: Much of the research on the interpretability of deep neural networks has focused on studying the visual features that maximally activate individual neurons. However, recent work has cast doubts on the usefulness of such local representations for understanding the behavior of deep neural networks because individual neurons tend to respond to multiple unrelated visual patterns, a phenomenon referred to as "superposition". A promising alternative to disentangle these complex patterns is learning sparsely distributed vector representations from entire network layers, as the resulting basis vectors seemingly encode single identifiable visual patterns consistently. Thus, one would expect the resulting code to align better with human perceivable visual patterns, but supporting evidence remains, at best, anecdotal. To fill this gap, we conducted three large-scale psychophysics experiments collected from a pool of 560 participants. Our findings provide (i) strong evidence that features obtained from sparse distributed representations are easier to interpret by human observers and (ii) that this effect is more pronounced in the deepest layers of a neural network. Complementary analyses also reveal that (iii) features derived from sparse distributed representations contribute more to the model's decision. Overall, our results highlight that distributed representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, underscoring a need for the field to move beyond the interpretation of local neural codes in favor of sparsely distributed ones.

papers.title: Interpreting intermediate convolutional layers of generative CNNs trained on waveforms
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize intermediate layers in generative CNNs trained on raw speech data to understand how acoustic properties and linguistic units are encoded?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a technique to interpret intermediate layers in generative CNNs trained on raw speech by averaging over feature maps after ReLU activation, which yields interpretable time-series data. It combines this with linear interpolation of the latent space to show causal relationships between latent variables and intermediate layer activations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed technique allows for detailed interpretation of how acoustic properties and linguistic units are encoded across the layers of generative CNNs trained on speech, revealing causal links between the latent space and intermediate representations.
papers.key_findings:
Averaging over feature maps after ReLU activation in transpose convolutional layers yields interpretable time-series data that can be acoustically analyzed (e.g., for F0, intensity, formants).
Different acoustic properties are encoded at different layers: intensity is encoded in earlier layers, F0 appears in later layers (Conv4), and formant structure is primarily encoded in the final output layer.
Linear interpolation of individual latent variables (e.g., corresponding to the presence of [s]) reveals a causal relationship between these variables and specific activations in intermediate layers.
The technique can be applied to study higher-level phonological processes like reduplication, showing how such patterns are encoded in the network.
The proposed method scales to deeper models, with similar encoding patterns observed in a 10-layer WaveGAN trained on LibriSpeech.
papers.limitation:
The models are trained on limited and curated data, and the technique is applied only to GAN-based models, not to more commonly used ASR/TTS models.
Formant structure is only encoded in the final layer of the 5-layer models, partly due to Nyquist frequency constraints in earlier layers.
future_direction: Apply the proposed technique to other CNN-based models used in ASR and TTS, such as wav2vec 2.0.
Apply the technique to Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) used in unsupervised speech technologies.
Use the technique as a diagnostic to improve CNN performance, e.g., by adding more layers to better encode higher-frequency properties like formants.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a technique to interpret and visualize intermediate layers in generative CNNs trained on raw speech data in an unsupervised manner. We argue that averaging over feature maps after ReLU activation in each transpose convolutional layer yields interpretable time-series data. This technique allows for acoustic analysis of intermediate layers that parallels the acoustic analysis of human speech data: we can extract F0, intensity, duration, formants, and other acoustic properties from intermediate layers in order to test where and how CNNs encode various types of information. We further combine this technique with linear interpolation of a model's latent space to show a causal relationship between individual variables in the latent space and activations in a model's intermediate convolutional layers. In particular, observing the causal effect between linear interpolation and the resulting changes in intermediate layers can reveal how individual latent variables get transformed into spikes in activation in intermediate layers. We train and probe internal representations of two models -- a bare WaveGAN architecture and a ciwGAN extension which forces the Generator to output informative data and results in the emergence of linguistically meaningful representations. Interpretation and visualization is performed for three basic acoustic properties of speech: periodic vibration (corresponding to vowels), aperiodic noise vibration (corresponding to fricatives), and silence (corresponding to stops). The proposal also allows testing of higher-level morphophonological alternations such as reduplication (copying). In short, using the proposed technique, we can analyze how linguistically meaningful units in speech get encoded in each convolutional layer of a generative neural network.

papers.title: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Echo State Networks applied to Earth System Variability
papers.research_question: How can Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to make them interpretable, and how does this apply to the detection of El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) can be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to interpret their decisions, and shows that the leak rate in the reservoir is a crucial parameter controlling memory and performance.
papers.conclusion: LRP can be applied to ESNs to open the black-box, and ESNs are effective for image classification tasks like ENSO detection, with advantages in training speed and parameter efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
LRP can be successfully applied to ESNs, providing relevance maps that highlight important input regions for classification.
The leak rate in the reservoir determines the memory time scale; too high leak rate causes the model to forget early inputs and performance drops.
ESNs achieve competitive accuracy with fewer trainable parameters compared to MLP, reducing overfitting risks.
The model focuses on the Niño 3.4 region for ENSO detection, which is physically reasonable.
The model is robust to random permutation of input columns, indicating it does not rely on the zonal structure of the data.
future_direction: Apply further xAI techniques (backward optimization, sensitivity analysis, salience maps) to ESN models.
Use ESN models for time series prediction with LRP as an alternative to attention mechanisms.
Apply ESNs with LRP to unsolved problems in climate and ocean science.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are known to be powerful methods for many hard problems (e.g. image classification, speech recognition or time series prediction). However, these models tend to produce black-box results and are often difficult to interpret. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is a widely used technique to understand how ANN models come to their conclusion and to understand what a model has learned. Here, we focus on Echo State Networks (ESNs) as a certain type of recurrent neural networks, also known as reservoir computing. ESNs are easy to train and only require a small number of trainable parameters, but are still black-box models. We show how LRP can be applied to ESNs in order to open the black-box. We also show how ESNs can be used not only for time series prediction but also for image classification: Our ESN model serves as a detector for El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies. ENSO is actually a well-known problem and has been extensively discussed before. But here we use this simple problem to demonstrate how LRP can significantly enhance the explainablility of ESNs.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: On Privileged and Convergent Bases in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the significance of feature directions represented by individual neurons in neural networks, and do networks converge to a unique basis across different training runs?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks do not naturally converge to a unique basis, but freezing early layers can enforce basis convergence, and linear mode connectivity improvements with width are not due to increased basis correlation.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks do not have a privileged basis that is unique across runs, but a convergent basis can be achieved by freezing early layers, which is useful for interpretability and modular training.
papers.key_findings:
perm-corr remains nearly constant across width, indicating no convergence to a unique basis.
LMC barrier decreases with width, but this improvement is not due to increased basis correlation.
Networks cannot learn rotationally invariant representations; random rotations degrade performance.
Freezing early layers increases basis correlation and reduces identity stitching penalty.
Basis correlation is higher when early layers are frozen identically.
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigate whether the representations learned by neural networks possess a privileged and convergent basis. Specifically, we examine the significance of feature directions represented by individual neurons. First, we establish that arbitrary rotations of neural representations cannot be inverted (unlike linear networks), indicating that they do not exhibit complete rotational invariance. Subsequently, we explore the possibility of multiple bases achieving identical performance. To do this, we compare the bases of networks trained with the same parameters but with varying random initializations. Our study reveals two findings: (1) Even in wide networks such as WideResNets, neural networks do not converge to a unique basis; (2) Basis correlation increases significantly when a few early layers of the network are frozen identically. Furthermore, we analyze Linear Mode Connectivity, which has been studied as a measure of basis correlation. Our findings give evidence that while Linear Mode Connectivity improves with increased network width, this improvement is not due to an increase in basis correlation.

papers.title: Understanding Generative AI Content with Embedding Models
papers.research_question: Can embedding vectors from foundation models reveal semantic distinctions in data, particularly separability between real and AI-generated samples?
papers.core_contribution: Embedding vectors from foundation models, when combined with dimensionality reduction, can separate real and AI-generated data, revealing inherent biases (generative DNA) in generative models.
papers.conclusion: Feature embedders can reveal statistical biases in generative models and provide a foundation for automated detection of AI-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
Embedding vectors from feature embedders (FEs) can separate data from different sources, including real vs. AI-generated.
The separability is due to differences in sampling techniques and generative model biases (generative DNA).
Even after normalization (e.g., translation), differences persist due to content and style.
Simple classifiers like Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) achieve high accuracy in distinguishing real and AI-generated data.
The signal in embedded data is low-dimensional, explaining why distributional shifts are easily detectable.
papers.limitation: For short text samples (e.g., one sentence), it is difficult to distinguish between human and machine translations.
papers.abstract: Constructing high-quality features is critical to any quantitative data analysis. While feature engineering was historically addressed by carefully hand-crafting data representations based on domain expertise, deep neural networks (DNNs) now offer a radically different approach. DNNs implicitly engineer features by transforming their input data into hidden feature vectors called embeddings. For embedding vectors produced by foundation models -- which are trained to be useful across many contexts -- we demonstrate that simple and well-studied dimensionality-reduction techniques such as Principal Component Analysis uncover inherent heterogeneity in input data concordant with human-understandable explanations. Of the many applications for this framework, we find empirical evidence that there is intrinsic separability between real samples and those generated by artificial intelligence (AI).

papers.title: Interpretability for Time Series Transformers using A Concept Bottleneck Framework
papers.research_question: How can we make time series transformers interpretable by steering them to learn predefined, interpretable concepts while maintaining forecasting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models and Centered Kernel Alignment to steer time series transformers to learn predefined interpretable concepts (e.g., a linear surrogate model and time features) in a designated bottleneck layer, improving interpretability without significantly harming forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: The concept bottleneck framework successfully improves the interpretability of time series transformers by encouraging specific components to align with human-understandable concepts, with minimal impact on forecasting accuracy, and enables faithful local interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework maintains model performance (MSE, MAE) on benchmark datasets while making the bottleneck layer's representations highly similar to the predefined concepts, as measured by CKA.
Component visualizations and activation patching interventions confirm that the bottleneck components learn and causally influence the model's predictions based on the intended concepts.
The framework is successfully applied to three different transformer architectures (Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer, FEDformer) on synthetic and real-world time series data.
Including a 'free' component in the bottleneck (not constrained by concepts) can help maintain performance and capture additional, non-predefined patterns in the data.
The intervention experiment demonstrates that the model's performance on time-shifted data can be restored by patching the activations of the time-concept component, confirming the causal role of the bottleneck.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes that relevant, interpretable concepts are known a priori and provided to the model.
The framework introduces additional computational cost during training due to the CKA loss calculation.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other types of sequential data beyond time series.
Exploring more complex or domain-specific interpretable concepts.
Investigating the use of the framework for model debugging and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability focuses on reverse engineering the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. We extend our focus and propose to mechanistically forward engineer using our framework based on Concept Bottleneck Models. In the context of long-term time series forecasting, we modify the training objective to encourage a model to develop representations which are similar to predefined, interpretable concepts using Centered Kernel Alignment. This steers the bottleneck components to learn the predefined concepts, while allowing other components to learn other, undefined concepts. We apply the framework to the Vanilla Transformer, Autoformer and FEDformer, and present an in-depth analysis on synthetic data and on a variety of benchmark datasets. We find that the model performance remains mostly unaffected, while the model shows much improved interpretability. Additionally, we verify the interpretation of the bottleneck components with an intervention experiment using activation patching.

papers.title: Improving Neuron-level Interpretability with White-box Language Models
papers.research_question: Can building sparsity directly into the language model architecture (via a white-box design) improve neuron-level interpretability compared to post-hoc methods like sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a white-box transformer-like architecture (crate) that embeds sparse coding directly into the model, leading to significantly improved neuron-level interpretability compared to standard transformers like GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: Replacing the standard transformer architecture with the white-box crate model significantly improves neuron-level interpretability, pointing towards a promising direction for building more interpretable foundation models with built-in sparse coding.
papers.key_findings:
crate achieves up to 103% relative improvement in neuron-level interpretability over GPT-2 across multiple evaluation metrics.
The improved interpretability is steady across different layers and model sizes.
crate's interpretability stems from its ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens.
crate has more optimal representations for interpretability than GPT-2, as applying sparse autoencoders (SAE) to crate yields smaller improvements than applying SAE to GPT-2.
crate can be steered without the reconstruction loss inherent in post-hoc SAE methods.
papers.limitation: The performance of crate on the next-token prediction task is not as good as GPT-2, potentially due to the introduction of sparsity.
future_direction: Investigate a better trade-off between performance and interpretability in language models with built-in sparsity.
Research more qualitative mechanisms in white-box language models and how to use them for downstream edits.
papers.abstract: Neurons in auto-regressive language models like GPT-2 can be interpreted by analyzing their activation patterns. Recent studies have shown that techniques such as dictionary learning, a form of post-hoc sparse coding, enhance this neuron-level interpretability. In our research, we are driven by the goal to fundamentally improve neural network interpretability by embedding sparse coding directly within the model architecture, rather than applying it as an afterthought. In our study, we introduce a white-box transformer-like architecture named Coding RAte TransformEr (CRATE), explicitly engineered to capture sparse, low-dimensional structures within data distributions. Our comprehensive experiments showcase significant improvements (up to 103% relative improvement) in neuron-level interpretability across a variety of evaluation metrics. Detailed investigations confirm that this enhanced interpretability is steady across different layers irrespective of the model size, underlining CRATE's robust performance in enhancing neural network interpretability. Further analysis shows that CRATE's increased interpretability comes from its enhanced ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens. These findings point towards a promising direction for creating white-box foundation models that excel in neuron-level interpretation.

papers.title: Mapping Knowledge Representations to Concepts: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: How do current methods extract internal knowledge representations in a neural network and map them to human-understandable concepts? Can Deductive-Nomological (D-N) explanation taxonomy and causal types of explanations be useful in order to analyse what can be expected, and not expected, from knowledge representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a targeted review of research that aims to associate internal neural network representations with human understandable concepts, and proposes using Deductive-Nomological explanations and theories of causality as a taxonomy to understand the capabilities and limitations of such explanations.
papers.conclusion: The review raises important questions about the goal of explanations and the type of knowledge extractable from neural networks, emphasizing the need to differentiate between understanding the trained model and providing actionable decisions. It argues for involving users to emphasize contextual dependence and refocus research on the limitations of ML systems.
papers.key_findings:
Methods for extracting knowledge representations are dominated by two approaches: Feature Based Attribution (FBA) for local understanding and Internal Knowledge Representation (IKR) extraction for global understanding.
There is an ambiguity in the goal of model explainability: understanding the ML model versus providing actionable explanations in the deployment domain.
The reviewed research lacks user studies, despite heavy reliance on human abilities to compare images and infer concepts.
Explanations that aim for intervention or counterfactual reasoning rely on causal relations, but these are only valid for the ML model in isolation and not necessarily for the real-world domain.
The Deductive-Nomological explanation taxonomy is found useful for analyzing what can be expected from neural network explanations, highlighting that current methods typically aim for kind-data or model-data relations, not theory-data or entity-data relations.
papers.limitation:
The choice to use the D-N model and Overton's schematic overview delimits the type of explanations aimed for and excludes pragmatic, inductive statistical, teleological, and historical explanations.
The understanding of the concept 'concept' is not well-grounded from an ontological and epistemological perspective.
future_direction: Conducting user studies that actively involve users to emphasize contextual dependence.
Combining IKR and FBA methods in studies aiming for a global meta-perspective of model understanding.

Using scientific explanations and theories to formulate falsifiable hypotheses and evaluate how well a trained ML model models the usage domain, moving beyond the idea that more data solves the problem of induction.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks builds to a large extent on their ability to create internal knowledge representations from real-world high-dimensional data, such as images, sound, or text. Approaches to extract and present these representations, in order to explain the neural network's decisions, is an active and multifaceted research field. To gain a deeper understanding of a central aspect of this field, we have performed a targeted review focusing on research that aims to associate internal representations with human understandable concepts. In doing this, we added a perspective on the existing research by using primarily deductive nomological explanations as a proposed taxonomy. We find this taxonomy and theories of causality, useful for understanding what can be expected, and not expected, from neural network explanations. The analysis additionally uncovers an ambiguity in the reviewed literature related to the goal of model explainability; is it understanding the ML model or, is it actionable explanations useful in the deployment domain?

papers.title: Physical Symmetries Embedded in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can physical constraints (such as symmetries and conservation laws) be embedded into neural network architectures to guarantee that predictions obey known physics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture (hub layer) that embeds physical constraints (symmetries and conservation laws) exactly into the network structure, guaranteeing that predictions satisfy the underlying physics without the need for explicit regularization terms.
papers.conclusion: Embedding physical constraints into neural networks via hub layers improves predictive power, training efficiency, and robustness, and is crucial for reliable predictions in data-scarce regimes.
papers.key_findings:
A hub layer can enforce even/odd symmetry in regression tasks, outperforming standard MLPs in preserving symmetry while fitting noisy data.
For energy-conserving regression, a hub layer that corrects the MLP prediction using Hamiltonian dynamics ensures energy conservation and closed phase-space trajectories.
An unsupervised symplectic neural network, designed by embedding Hamilton's equations, conserves energy when solving differential equations and converges faster than a standard MLP.
future_direction: Embed other important symmetries into neural networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are a central technique in machine learning. Recent years have seen a wave of interest in applying neural networks to physical systems for which the governing dynamics are known and expressed through differential equations. Two fundamental challenges facing the development of neural networks in physics applications is their lack of interpretability and their physics-agnostic design. The focus of the present work is to embed physical constraints into the structure of the neural network to address the second fundamental challenge. By constraining tunable parameters (such as weights and biases) and adding special layers to the network, the desired constraints are guaranteed to be satisfied without the need for explicit regularization terms. This is demonstrated on upervised and unsupervised networks for two basic symmetries: even/odd symmetry of a function and energy conservation. In the supervised case, the network with embedded constraints is shown to perform well on regression problems while simultaneously obeying the desired constraints whereas a traditional network fits the data but violates the underlying constraints. Finally, a new unsupervised neural network is proposed that guarantees energy conservation through an embedded symplectic structure. The symplectic neural network is used to solve a system of energy-conserving differential equations and out-performs an unsupervised, non-symplectic neural network.

papers.title: KAN We Improve on HEP Classification Tasks? Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks Applied to an LHC Physics Example
papers.research_question: Can Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) improve performance and interpretability for high-energy physics classification tasks compared to multilayer perceptrons (MLPs)?
papers.core_contribution: For the studied HEP classification task, KANs are not more parameter efficient than MLPs, but small KANs offer interpretability advantages with only a moderate loss in performance.
papers.conclusion: KANs are a promising alternative for HEP classification tasks when interpretability is desired and moderate performance loss is acceptable, but more research is needed on deeper KANs and other applications.
papers.key_findings:
In a one-layer KAN, the learned activation functions resemble the univariate log-likelihood ratios of the input features.
In deeper KANs, the first-layer activations differ from those in one-layer KANs, indicating learning of more complex representations.
KANs and MLPs achieve similar classification performance for this task.
MLPs outperform KANs for very low numbers of trainable parameters.
Small KANs offer better interpretability than MLPs, but interpretability becomes challenging for deeper or wider KANs.
papers.limitation: The interpretability of deeper KANs is not explored in depth and remains challenging.
future_direction: Explore interpretability of deeper KANs using mechanistic interpretability techniques.
Apply symbolic regression to approximate learned activation functions.
Assess KAN performance and interpretability in HEP regression tasks.
papers.abstract: Abstract Recently, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have been proposed as an alternative to multilayer perceptrons, suggesting advantages in performance and interpretability. We study a typical binary event classification task in high-energy physics including high-level features and comment on the performance and interpretability of KANs in this context. Consistent with expectations, we find that the learned activation functions of a one-layer KAN resemble the univariate log-likelihood ratios of the respective input features. In deeper KANs, the activations in the first layer differ from those in the one-layer KAN, which indicates that the deeper KANs learn more complex representations of the data, a pattern commonly observed in other deep-learning architectures. We study KANs with different depths and widths and we compare them to multilayer perceptrons in terms of performance and number of trainable parameters. For the chosen classification task, we do not find that KANs are more parameter efficient. However, small KANs may offer advantages in terms of interpretability that come at the cost of only a moderate loss in performance.

papers.title: Nonlocal Attention Operator: Materializing Hidden Knowledge Towards Interpretable Physics Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we design an attention-based neural operator that simultaneously solves forward and inverse PDE problems, providing interpretability and generalizability to unseen physical systems?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Nonlocal Attention Operator (NAO), a novel neural operator architecture that uses an attention-based kernel map to simultaneously solve forward (modeling) and inverse (discovery) PDE problems, offering interpretability and zero-shot generalizability to new physical systems.
papers.conclusion: NAO is an effective neural operator architecture for simultaneously learning forward and inverse PDE solvers from data, providing interpretability through the discovered kernel and zero-shot generalizability to new physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
NAO achieves lower operator and kernel errors compared to discrete and softmax attention variants in forward and inverse PDE tasks.
NAO generalizes to unseen physical systems (zero-shot learning) and across different data resolutions.
The attention mechanism acts as a data-driven regularizer, resolving the ill-posedness of inverse PDE problems by exploring a function space of identifiability.
NAO's kernel map provides interpretability by revealing the hidden physical mechanism (kernel) from data.
NAO outperforms baseline models (Discrete-NAO, Softmax-NAO, NAO-u, AFNO, Autoencoder) in terms of generalizability and accuracy.
papers.limitation: Experiments focus on learning from a small to medium number (<500) of similar physical systems due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Expand the coverage to enable learning across different types of physical systems.
Build a foundation model in scientific machine learning.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent popularity of attention-based neural architectures in core AI fields like natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV), their potential in modeling complex physical systems remains under-explored. Learning problems in physical systems are often characterized as discovering operators that map between function spaces based on a few instances of function pairs. This task frequently presents a severely ill-posed PDE inverse problem. In this work, we propose a novel neural operator architecture based on the attention mechanism, which we coin Nonlocal Attention Operator (NAO), and explore its capability towards developing a foundation physical model. In particular, we show that the attention mechanism is equivalent to a double integral operator that enables nonlocal interactions among spatial tokens, with a data-dependent kernel characterizing the inverse mapping from data to the hidden parameter field of the underlying operator. As such, the attention mechanism extracts global prior information from training data generated by multiple systems, and suggests the exploratory space in the form of a nonlinear kernel map. Consequently, NAO can address ill-posedness and rank deficiency in inverse PDE problems by encoding regularization and achieving generalizability. We empirically demonstrate the advantages of NAO over baseline neural models in terms of generalizability to unseen data resolutions and system states. Our work not only suggests a novel neural operator architecture for learning interpretable foundation models of physical systems, but also offers a new perspective towards understanding the attention mechanism. Our code and data accompanying this paper are available at https://github.com/fishmoon1234/NAO.

papers.title: Interpretability of artificial neural network models in artificial Intelligence vs. neuroscience
papers.research_question: What are the different notions of interpretability in artificial intelligence and neuroscience, and how can neuroscientific interpretability be pursued independently?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that interpretability in AI and neuroscience are distinct, with neuroscientific interpretability requiring alignment between model components and brain constructs, and proposes that brain alignment can serve as a benchmark for evaluating AI explainability methods.
papers.conclusion: The authors encourage researchers to conceptually separate the objectives of AI and neuroscience interpretability, but suggest that AI interpretability methods aligned with primate brain interpretations are more promising.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is a multi-faceted construct used differently in AI (focusing on model component contributions to output) and neuroscience (requiring alignment with brain constructs).
Neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs is relative and depends on the model's intended use and the grain of analysis, with no need for full brain alignment if only specific experimental variables are of interest.
Current ANN models of primate vision contain features not mapped to neuroscientific constructs, limiting their neuroscientific interpretability.
Brain alignment (similarity with primate behavior and neural measurements) can validate the 'goodness' of AI explainability methods in the absence of ground truth.
AI interpretability methods that provide more primate-brain-aligned model interpretations are likely more promising, despite operational differences from brains.
papers.abstract: Computationally explicit hypotheses of brain function derived from machine learning (ML)-based models have recently revolutionized neuroscience. Despite the unprecedented ability of these artificial neural networks (ANNs) to capture responses in biological neural networks (brains), and our full access to all internal model components (unlike the brain), ANNs are often referred to as black-boxes with limited interpretability. Interpretability, however, is a multi-faceted construct that is used differently across fields. In particular, interpretability, or explainability, efforts in Artificial Intelligence (AI) focus on understanding how different model components contribute to its output (i.e., decision making). In contrast, the neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs requires explicit alignment between model components and neuroscientific constructs (e.g., different brain areas or phenomena, like recurrence or top-down feedback). Given the widespread calls to improve the interpretability of AI systems, we here highlight these different notions of interpretability and argue that the neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs can be pursued in parallel with, but independently from, the ongoing efforts in AI. Certain ML techniques (e.g., deep dream) can be leveraged in both fields, to ask what stimulus optimally activates the specific model features (feature visualization by optimization), or how different features contribute to the model's output (feature attribution). However, without appropriate brain alignment, certain features will remain uninterpretable to neuroscientists.

papers.title: Contrastive Explanations In Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can visual explanations for neural networks be extended to answer contrastive questions of the form 'Why P, rather than Q?' instead of just 'Why P?'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the structure of contrastive visual explanations for neural networks and proposes a methodology to extract contrasts from networks, which can be used as a plug-in on top of existing explanatory methods like Grad-CAM to answer 'Why P, rather than Q?' questions.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes contrastive explanations and provides a methodology to extract contrasts from neural networks, enabling their use as plug-in techniques for existing visual explanatory methods to answer contrastive questions.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive explanations can highlight discriminative features between similar classes in fine-grained recognition, such as differences in neck shape between spoonbills and flamingos.
The method is applicable to both classification and regression networks, demonstrated in recognition and image quality assessment tasks.
In image quality assessment, contrastive explanations localize regions that cause quality degradation or improvement, focusing on foreground distortions more than background.
Contrastive explanations provide context-specific insights by answering contrastive questions, making them more descriptive than standard 'Why P?' explanations.
The approach can be integrated with existing gradient-based explanation techniques like Grad-CAM without modifying the underlying network architecture.
papers.abstract: Visual explanations are logical arguments based on visual features that justify the predictions made by neural networks. Current modes of visual explanations answer questions of the form `Why P.7'. These Why questions operate under broad contexts thereby providing answers that are irrelevant in some cases. We propose to constrain these Why questions based on some context Q so that our explanations answer contrastive questions of the form `Why P, rather than Q.7'. In this paper, we formalize the structure of contrastive visual explanations for neural networks. We define contrast based on neural networks and propose a methodology to extract defined contrasts. We then use the extracted contrasts as a plug-in on top of existing `Why P?' techniques, specifically Grad-CAM. We demonstrate their value in analyzing both networks and data in applications of large-scale recognition, fine-grained recognition, subsurface seismic analysis, and image quality assessment.

papers.title: Scale Alone Does not Improve Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision Models
papers.research_question: Does scaling model and dataset size improve the mechanistic interpretability of vision models at the level of individual units?
papers.core_contribution: Scaling model and dataset size does not improve the mechanistic interpretability of vision models at the level of individual units, and latest-generation models may even be less interpretable than older ones.
papers.conclusion: Scale alone does not improve mechanistic interpretability in vision models; explicit design for interpretability is needed, and the released dataset can facilitate research on automated interpretability measures.
papers.key_findings:
No practically relevant differences in interpretability across nine vision models of varying scales, indicating that scaling does not improve interpretability.
Feature visualizations are less helpful than natural exemplars for explaining unit activations across all models, including adversarially robust models.
Interpretability does not increase with model classification performance or human-likeness, and may even decrease for feature visualizations as accuracy increases.
For models pre-trained on large datasets (Clip ResNet and Clip ViT), later layers are more interpretable, suggesting a shift in interpretability across layers.
Interpretability drops sharply when the task difficulty increases slightly, indicating that human understanding of unit behavior is limited.
papers.limitation:
The study only employed two widely-used explanation methods (feature visualizations and natural exemplars), which may not capture all aspects of interpretability.
Feature visualizations for ViT models were not evaluated due to methodological challenges, limiting the comparison for transformer architectures.
future_direction: Designing models explicitly for interpretability rather than relying on scale.
Developing automated interpretability measures using the released dataset to avoid costly human evaluations.
Further research on interpretability methods beyond feature visualizations and natural exemplars.
papers.abstract: In light of the recent widespread adoption of AI systems, understanding the internal information processing of neural networks has become increasingly critical. Most recently, machine vision has seen remarkable progress by scaling neural networks to unprecedented levels in dataset and model size. We here ask whether this extraordinary increase in scale also positively impacts the field of mechanistic interpretability. In other words, has our understanding of the inner workings of scaled neural networks improved as well? We use a psychophysical paradigm to quantify one form of mechanistic interpretability for a diverse suite of nine models and find no scaling effect for interpretability - neither for model nor dataset size. Specifically, none of the investigated state-of-the-art models are easier to interpret than the GoogLeNet model from almost a decade ago. Latest-generation vision models appear even less interpretable than older architectures, hinting at a regression rather than improvement, with modern models sacrificing interpretability for accuracy. These results highlight the need for models explicitly designed to be mechanistically interpretable and the need for more helpful interpretability methods to increase our understanding of networks at an atomic level. We release a dataset containing more than 130'000 human responses from our psychophysical evaluation of 767 units across nine models. This dataset facilitates research on automated instead of human-based interpretability evaluations, which can ultimately be leveraged to directly optimize the mechanistic interpretability of models.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the interpretability of latent representations in CNNs by measuring the alignment between individual hidden units and semantic concepts, and what factors affect this interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Network Dissection, a framework for quantifying the interpretability of CNN representations by evaluating the alignment between individual convolutional units and a broad set of semantic concepts, and uses it to show interpretability is an axis-aligned property affected by architecture, training data, and regularization.
papers.conclusion: Network Dissection provides a method to quantify interpretability in CNNs, revealing that interpretability is an axis-aligned property indicative of partially disentangled representations, and is influenced by network architecture, training data, and training techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability of units is not axis-independent; random rotations of the representation significantly reduce the number of unique concept detectors, indicating interpretability is a special alignment learned by the network.
Deeper network architectures (ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet) and training on scene-centric data (Places) lead to more interpretable units (more unique concept detectors).
Self-supervised training tasks produce fewer object detectors and more texture detectors compared to supervised training, and the form of self-supervision (e.g., colorization) affects which concepts emerge.
Batch normalization significantly reduces interpretability, while dropout and different random initializations have less impact on the final level of interpretability.
Widening a convolutional layer (increasing the number of units) can increase the number of unique concept detectors without significantly harming classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: Network dissection works only as well as the underlying dataset; if a unit matches a human-understandable concept that is absent in Broden, it will not score well for interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the Broden dataset to include more kinds of visual concepts.
Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
papers.abstract: We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN model, the proposed method draws on a data set of concepts to score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer. The units with semantics are labeled across a broad range of visual concepts including objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the hypothesis that interpretability is an axis-independent property of the representation space, then we apply the method to compare the latent representations of various networks when trained to solve different classification problems. We further analyze the effect of training iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, and measure the effect of dropout and batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative power.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
