papers.research_question: Can empirical adjustments to transformation structure lead to more stable, analyzable learning behavior without global architectural redesign?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neural architecture with structured transformations and adaptive corrections, improving stability, interpretability, and robustness in training.
papers.conclusion: The proposed structured transformation with corrective pathways leads to more tractable and resilient learning systems, suggesting that internal organization can enhance reliability without sacrificing expressivity.
papers.key_findings:
Improved gradient conditioning and smooth gradient flow compared to standard MLPs.
Enhanced robustness to input perturbations and noise.
Stable activation variance and broader neuron participation during training.
Predictable convergence dynamics under recursive application of modules.
Scalable up to 10 layers without skip connections or normalization, with graceful degradation beyond.
papers.limitation:
The model becomes unstable beyond 10 layers without skip connections or normalization.
Interpretability studies and theoretical extensions are deferred to follow-up work.
future_direction: Further interpretability studies of the structured transformations.
Theoretical extensions to formalize the stability properties.
Broader application of the principles to more complex architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive performance, contemporary neural networks often lack structural safeguards that promote stable learning and interpretable behavior. In this work, we introduce a reformulation of layer-level transformations that departs from the standard unconstrained affine paradigm. Each transformation is decomposed into a structured linear operator and a residual corrective component, enabling more disciplined signal propagation and improved training dynamics. Our formulation encourages internal consistency and supports stable information flow across depth, while remaining fully compatible with standard learning objectives and backpropagation. Through a series of synthetic and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that models constructed with these structured transformations exhibit improved gradient conditioning, reduced sensitivity to perturbations, and layer-wise robustness. We further show that these benefits persist across architectural scales and training regimes. This study serves as a foundation for a more principled class of neural architectures that prioritize stability and transparency-offering new tools for reasoning about learning behavior without sacrificing expressive power.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: TURBO: The Swiss Knife of Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of the Information Bottleneck (IBN) principle for explaining auto-encoding methods, and can a new framework (TURBO) provide a more comprehensive theoretical foundation that generalizes a wider range of models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the TURBO framework, a novel information-theoretic formulation that maximizes mutual information between two data representations, providing a unifying theoretical explanation for a broad family of auto-encoder models (including VAE, GAN, AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN) where the Information Bottleneck principle falls short.
papers.conclusion: The TURBO framework serves as a powerful and versatile theoretical tool that unifies a wide spectrum of auto-encoding models, offering a richer understanding of data representation and neural network structure beyond the limitations of the Information Bottleneck principle.
papers.key_findings:
The Information Bottleneck (IBN) principle has inherent limitations, particularly when data has multiple relevant representations or when the latent space is physically meaningful rather than a compressed virtual space.
The TURBO framework, based on maximizing mutual information in two directions (direct and reverse paths), generalizes and provides a rigorous interpretation for models like AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN, and normalizing flows, which the IBN principle struggles to explain.
TURBO's loss function decomposes into reconstruction and distribution matching terms, allowing it to seamlessly handle paired, unpaired, and partially paired data scenarios.
Many well-known models (VAE, GAN, AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN, Flows) are shown to be special cases of the TURBO framework, each corresponding to a specific subset of its loss terms.
The framework enables new applications, such as linking physically meaningful modalities (e.g., particle momenta to detector responses) and transcoding between different data representations.
papers.abstract: We present a novel information-theoretic framework, termed as TURBO, designed to systematically analyse and generalise auto-encoding methods. We start by examining the principles of information bottleneck and bottleneck-based networks in the auto-encoding setting and identifying their inherent limitations, which become more prominent for data with multiple relevant, physics-related representations. The TURBO framework is then introduced, providing a comprehensive derivation of its core concept consisting of the maximisation of mutual information between various data representations expressed in two directions reflecting the information flows. We illustrate that numerous prevalent neural network models are encompassed within this framework. The paper underscores the insufficiency of the information bottleneck concept in elucidating all such models, thereby establishing TURBO as a preferable theoretical reference. The introduction of TURBO contributes to a richer understanding of data representation and the structure of neural network models, enabling more efficient and versatile applications.

papers.title: The Interpretable Dictionary in Sparse Coding
papers.research_question: Does sparse coding under sparsity constraints yield more interpretable neural networks compared to standard deep learning models?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse coding with sparsity constraints produces more interpretable neural networks than standard deep learning, as demonstrated by selective activations and lower cross-correlation in dictionary elements.
papers.conclusion: Sparse coding with elements of sparsity, competition, and selectivity leads to interpretable models where each neuron's contribution can be directly determined, unlike deep learning models where explanations are confounded by dense activations.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse coding dictionary elements are interpretable and correspond to semantic features in information graphics.
Activations in sparse coding are sparse and selective, activating only for relevant image patches, unlike CNN activations which are dense and non-specific.
Cross-correlation analysis shows that sparse coding has significantly lower mean intra- and inter-image correlation compared to CNN filters.
The sparse coding model achieves high sparsity with around 4% of elements active per image and low frequency of usage per dictionary element.
Qualitative comparisons show that sparse coding activations directly attribute image components to specific dictionary elements, enabling clear explanations.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs), specifically deep learning networks, have often been labeled as black boxes due to the fact that the internal representation of the data is not easily interpretable. In our work, we illustrate that an ANN, trained using sparse coding under specific sparsity constraints, yields a more interpretable model than the standard deep learning model. The dictionary learned by sparse coding can be more easily understood and the activations of these elements creates a selective feature output. We compare and contrast our sparse coding model with an equivalent feed forward convolutional autoencoder trained on the same data. Our results show both qualitative and quantitative benefits in the interpretation of the learned sparse coding dictionary as well as the internal activation representations.

papers.title: Interpretability in Linear Brain Decoding
papers.research_question: What is a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models, and how can we quantitatively evaluate interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models and proposes a multi-objective criterion combining interpretability and performance for model selection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed definition provides a theoretical background for the quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.
papers.key_findings:
In noisy data, the most accurate linear decoding model is not necessarily the most interpretable, highlighting a trade-off between performance and interpretability.
Incorporating the proposed interpretability measure into model selection can lead to more interpretable models when using regularization techniques like Lasso.
papers.limitation:
The definition of interpretability is theoretical and assumes the true solution of the brain decoding problem is available, which is not realistic in practice.
The definition and quantification are limited to linear models; extending to non-linear models requires future research.
future_direction: Extending the definition of interpretability to non-linear models.
papers.abstract: Improving the interpretability of brain decoding approaches is of primary interest in many neuroimaging studies. Despite extensive studies of this type, at present, there is no formal definition for interpretability of brain decoding models. As a consequence, there is no quantitative measure for evaluating the interpretability of different brain decoding methods. In this paper, we present a simple definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models. Then, we propose to combine the interpretability and the performance of the brain decoding into a new multi-objective criterion for model selection. Our preliminary results on the toy data show that optimizing the hyper-parameters of the regularized linear classifier based on the proposed criterion results in more informative linear models. The presented definition provides the theoretical background for quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: Discovering and Steering Interpretable Concepts in Large Generative Music Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and interpret the internal concepts learned by autoregressive music generation models, and can we use these concepts to steer generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline using sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable concepts in autoregressive music models, and shows that these concepts can be used to steer generation.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility and potential of using sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable concepts in large music generative models, offering a scalable path towards understanding how these models represent and generate music.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can discover both familiar musical concepts (e.g., genres, instruments) and novel coherent patterns lacking clear theoretical description.
Later layers in the model encode more interpretable features on average, as measured by CLAP alignment with automatic labels.
Larger models (MusicGen-Large) produce features that are more distinctive by layer compared to smaller models (MusicGen-Small).
Automated labeling using Essentia classifiers and multimodal LLMs (Gemini) can label thousands of features at scale, with Essentia tags achieving higher human confidence.
A non-trivial fraction (15-35%) of discovered features can be used to steer model generations, altering outputs toward the intended concept.
papers.limitation: The analysis focuses on unconditional audio representations, not text-conditioned activations, which limits understanding of how prompts influence internal concepts.
future_direction: Extending the method to text-conditioned activations and multimodal interpretability.
Building a comprehensive understanding of how neural networks represent and generate music.
papers.abstract: The fidelity with which neural networks can now generate content such as music presents a scientific opportunity: these systems appear to have learned implicit theories of such content's structure through statistical learning alone. This offers a potentially new lens on theories of human-generated media. When internal representations align with traditional constructs (e.g. chord progressions in music), they show how such categories can emerge from statistical regularities; when they diverge, they expose limits of existing frameworks and patterns we may have overlooked but that nonetheless carry explanatory power. In this paper, focusing on music generators, we introduce a method for discovering interpretable concepts using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), extracting interpretable features from the residual stream of a transformer model. We make this approach scalable and evaluable using automated labeling and validation pipelines. Our results reveal both familiar musical concepts and coherent but uncodified patterns lacking clear counterparts in theory or language. As an extension, we show such concepts can be used to steer model generations. Beyond improving model transparency, our work provides an empirical tool for uncovering organizing principles that have eluded traditional methods of analysis and synthesis.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators: Model Recovery in Function Spaces
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be extended to operate in infinite-dimensional function spaces for concept learning, and what advantages do functional representations offer over standard SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs) that operate in function spaces, specifically SAE-FNOs, which improve concept learning stability, robustness, and generalization compared to standard SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Functional representations in SAE-NOs extend sparse autoencoders from detectors of concept presence to models that capture the underlying structure of the data, highlighting parameterization as a central driver of interpretability and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-FNO successfully recovers ground-truth concepts in synthetic data and converges to zero dictionary recovery error.
SAE-FNO generalizes to unseen input resolutions, unlike SAE-CNN which fails beyond training resolution.
SAE-FNO learns concepts that are stable across different sparsity levels and exhibit diverse correlations, overcoming the orthogonality bias of SAE-MLP.
SAE-FNO achieves higher concept utilization efficiency, requiring fewer concepts to represent data, especially for larger domains.
Lifting accelerates concept recovery by acting as a preconditioner and improves optimization.
papers.abstract: We frame the problem of unifying representations in neural models as one of sparse model recovery and introduce a framework that extends sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to lifted spaces and infinite-dimensional function spaces, enabling mechanistic interpretability of large neural operators (NO). While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that neural networks converge to similar representations across architectures, the representational properties of neural operators remain underexplored despite their growing importance in scientific computing. We compare the inference and training dynamics of SAEs, lifted-SAE, and SAE neural operators. We highlight how lifting and operator modules introduce beneficial inductive biases, enabling faster recovery, improved recovery of smooth concepts, and robust inference across varying resolutions, a property unique to neural operators.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Real Sparks of Artificial Intelligence and the Importance of Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: Is black-box interpretability sufficient for attributing intelligence to AI models, and how can inner interpretability provide a better assessment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that black-box interpretability is insufficient for attributing intelligence to AI models because it ignores how processes are carried out, and advocates for inner interpretability (mechanistic interpretability) as a necessary approach to determine whether models are truly intelligent (i.e., manipulating symbols based on meaning).
papers.conclusion: Inner interpretability is a better approach than black-box interpretability for assessing intelligence in AI models, and philosophy can contribute valuable concepts and theories to guide this research.
papers.key_findings:
Black-box interpretability, as exemplified by Bubeck et al.'s work on GPT-4, is flawed because it lacks the epistemic buttressing we have when attributing intelligence to humans and animals, and it cannot distinguish between intelligent processes and mere mimicry.
Inner interpretability can reveal the internal mechanisms of models, such as circuits and representations, which are crucial for assessing whether the model is implementing intelligent processes.
Examples from Wang et al. (circuit discovery in GPT-2 small) and Li et al. (emergent world representations in Othello-GPT) demonstrate how inner interpretability can uncover mechanisms that may or may not indicate intelligent processing.
Philosophical theories, such as Dretske's account of representation and cognition, can guide inner interpretability by emphasizing the importance of semantic sensitivity and the manipulation of symbols based on their meaning.
The paper suggests that inner interpretability, combined with philosophical insights, can lead to better assessments of intelligence, interpretability, and ethical implications of AI models.
future_direction: Investigating cognitive processes and intelligence in AI models through inner interpretability.
Developing robust interpretability that includes psychological explanations (person-level explanations) for AI behavior.
Exploring the ethical ramifications of AI models by using inner interpretability to detect biased or harmful representations and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: The present paper looks at one of the most thorough articles on the intelligence of GPT, research conducted by engineers at Microsoft. Although there is a great deal of value in their work, I will argue that, for familiar philosophical reasons, their methodology, !Blackbox Interpretability"#is wrongheaded. But there is a better way. There is an exciting and emerging discipline of !Inner Interpretability"#(and specifically Mechanistic Interpretability) that aims to uncover the internal activations and weights of models in order to understand what they represent and the algorithms they implement. In my view, a crucial mistake in Black-box Interpretability is the failure to appreciate that how processes are carried out matters when it comes to intelligence and understanding. I can#t pretend to have a full story that provides both necessary and sufficient conditions for being intelligent, but I do think that Inner Interpretability dovetails nicely with plausible philosophical views of what intelligence requires. So the conclusion is modest, but the important point in my view is seeing how to get the research on the right track. Towards the end of the paper, I will show how some of the philosophical concepts can be used to further refine how Inner Interpretability is approached, so the paper helps draw out a profitable, future two-way exchange between Philosophers and Computer Scientists.

papers.title: Interpretable Neural Networks based classifiers for categorical inputs
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the output of neural network classifiers that take categorical inputs by expanding the network's function as a sum of contributions from input patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network classifiers for categorical inputs by expanding the network's output function as a polynomial sum of contributions from input patterns, which can be interpreted as an energy model and related to maximum entropy models.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a global interpretation of neural network classifiers for categorical inputs, and lower-order terms often dominate, allowing for approximate interpretations. The method can be extended to real-valued inputs with approximations.
papers.key_findings:
The output of a neural network classifier with categorical inputs can be exactly represented as a finite polynomial expansion.
The coefficients of the expansion can be computed via derivatives or perturbations at the zero input.
Applying an Ising gauge transformation emphasizes lower-order terms.
In the MNIST example, first and second order terms capture most of the network's behavior.
In the protein sequence prediction, first order terms are often sufficient, but second order terms can improve predictions and reveal three-body interactions.
papers.limitation: The method is exact only for categorical inputs and for networks with C∞ activation functions; for real-valued inputs the expansion is infinite and only approximate.
future_direction: Apply the technique to the study of protein sequences.
Extend the method to real-valued inputs for approximate interpretations.
Investigate robustness to adversarial attacks using the reduced description.
papers.abstract: Because of the pervasive usage of Neural Networks in human sensitive applications, their interpretability is becoming an increasingly important topic in machine learning. In this work we introduce a simple way to interpret the output function of a neural network classifier that take as input categorical variables. By exploiting a mapping between a neural network classifier and a physical energy model, we show that in these cases each layer of the network, and the logits layer in particular, can be expanded as a sum of terms that account for the contribution to the classification of each input pattern. For instance, at the first order, the expansion considers just the linear relation between input features and output while at the second order pairwise dependencies between input features are also accounted for. The analysis of the contributions of each pattern, after an appropriate gauge transformation, is presented in two cases where the effectiveness of the method can be appreciated.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Large Language Model Alignment: Progress, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.research_question: This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examines how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies, and identifies key challenges and future research directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability techniques for LLM alignment, analyzing progress, challenges, and future directions.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability is essential for understanding and aligning LLMs, but fundamental challenges remain. Future work must focus on scalable automated methods, rigorous validation, and pluralistic alignment that respects diverse human values.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability has enabled targeted interventions for alignment, such as steering model behavior and identifying harmful circuits.
Fundamental challenges include superposition, polysemanticity, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models.
Interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies like RLHF, constitutional AI, and scalable oversight.
Future research should focus on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization, and interpretability-driven alignment techniques.
The field must address pluralistic alignment to respect diverse human values and cultures.
papers.limitation:
False confidence: Interpretability might provide misleading confidence in model safety if interpretations are incorrect or incomplete.
Arms race dynamics: Interpretability tools could be used to make models better at deception or to remove safety mechanisms.
Diminishing returns: The cost of interpretability may grow faster than model capabilities, potentially making comprehensive understanding of future systems intractable.
Philosophical challenges: Even perfect interpretability may not resolve fundamental questions about consciousness, moral status, or value alignment in AI systems.
future_direction: Automated interpretability at scale, including scalable circuit discovery and automated description generation.
Cross-model generalization, investigating universal circuits and transfer of interventions.
Interpretability-first alignment, including mechanistic anomaly detection and transparent architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, yet their internal decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Mechanistic interpretability (i.e., the systematic study of how neural networks implement algorithms through their learned representations and computational structures) has emerged as a critical research direction for understanding and aligning these models. This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examining methods ranging from circuit discovery to feature visualization, activation steering, and causal intervention. We analyze how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies including reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), constitutional AI, and scalable oversight. Key challenges are identified, including the superposition hypothesis, polysemanticity of neurons, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models. We propose future research directions focusing on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization of circuits, and the development of interpretability-driven alignment techniques that can scale to frontier models.

papers.title: Neural Harmonium: An Interpretable Deep Structure for Nonlinear Dynamic System Identification with Application to Audio Processing
papers.research_question: How to design an interpretable deep structure for nonlinear dynamic system identification that combines neural networks and adaptive filtering in a time-frequency domain?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neural Harmonium, an interpretable deep structure for nonlinear dynamic system identification that combines neural networks and adaptive filtering in a time-frequency domain, enabling efficient second-order optimization and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Neural Harmonium is an effective interpretable hybrid structure for modeling nonlinear multistage dynamical systems in real-life applications, combining the strengths of deep neural networks and adaptive filtering.
papers.key_findings:
Neural Harmonium outperforms Wiener-Hammerstein, Gaussian process regression, and nonlinear ARX models in modeling magnetic hysteresis, achieving a modeling error of -15.93 dB.
The method effectively models amplitude modulation, achieving a modeling error of -32.96 dB, significantly better than an ARX baseline.
In acoustic echo cancellation, Neural Harmonium achieves high ERLE (35.79 dB) and PESQ (0.43) scores, performing on par with a DNN-based interference suppression method.
Subjective evaluation via MOS shows Neural Harmonium scores well for both speech (3.24) and music (2.78) near-end signals in echo cancellation scenarios.
The dependency maps generated by the neural network component provide interpretable insights into the frequency interdependencies of the nonlinear system.
papers.abstract: Improving the interpretability of deep neural networks has recently gained increased attention, especially when the power of deep learning is leveraged to solve problems in physics. Interpretability helps us understand a model's ability to generalize and reveal its limitations. In this paper, we introduce a causal interpretable deep structure for modeling dynamic systems. Our proposed model makes use of the harmonic analysis by modeling the system in a time-frequency domain while maintaining high temporal and spectral resolution. Moreover, the model is built in an order recursive manner which allows for fast, robust, and exact second order optimization without the need for an explicit Hessian calculation. To circumvent the resulting high dimensionality of the building blocks of our system, a neural network is designed to identify the frequency interdependencies. The proposed model is illustrated and validated on nonlinear system identification problems as required for audio signal processing tasks. Crowd-sourced experimentation contrasting the performance of the proposed approach to other state-of-the-art solutions on an acoustic echo cancellation scenario confirms the effectiveness of our method for real-life applications.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: Is This Just Fantasy? Language Model Representations Reflect Human Judgments of Event Plausibility
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable)? How do these representations develop, do they reflect human categorization behavior, and what interpretable features do they correspond to?
papers.core_contribution: Language models form linear representations (modal difference vectors) that distinguish between modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable). These vectors are more diagnostic than output probabilities, emerge in an intuitive order during training, and reflect fine-grained human categorization behavior and interpretable features like event likelihood and imageability.
papers.conclusion: Language models learn internal representations of modal categories that go beyond output probabilities. These representations develop in an intuitive order and capture nuanced aspects of human categorization, offering a novel way to study world models in LMs and potentially human cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Modal difference vectors within LM hidden states reliably classify sentences by modal category, outperforming classification based on sentence probability.
Modal difference vectors develop in a consistent order: inconceivable vs. others emerges first, followed by probable vs. impossible, then probable vs. improbable, and finally improbable vs. impossible.
Projections of sentences onto modal difference vectors create a feature space that accurately models human participants' graded categorization judgments.
Projections along the impossible-inconceivable vector correlate selectively with human ratings of imageability and the presence of physical objects/places.
Preliminary steering experiments show that adding modal difference vectors to the residual stream during generation can influence the modal category of the generated text.
future_direction: Using modal difference vectors to test the intuitive theories about the world that LMs encode from text.
Using modal difference vectors to generate hypotheses about human representations of modal categories, such as the role of imagination in distinguishing impossible from inconceivable events.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are used for a diverse range of tasks, from question answering to writing fantastical stories. In order to reliably accomplish these tasks, LMs must be able to discern the modal category of a sentence (i.e., whether it describes something that is possible, impossible, completely nonsensical, etc.). However, recent studies have called into question the ability of LMs to categorize sentences according to modality (Michaelov et al., 2025; Kauf et al., 2023). In this work, we identify linear representations that discriminate between modal categories within a variety of LMs, or modal difference vectors. Analysis of modal difference vectors reveals that LMs have access to more reliable modal categorization judgments than previously reported. Furthermore, we find that modal difference vectors emerge in a consistent order as models become more competent (i.e., through training steps, layers, and parameter count). Notably, we find that modal difference vectors identified within LM activations can be used to model fine-grained human categorization behavior. This potentially provides a novel view into how human participants distinguish between modal categories, which we explore by correlating projections along modal difference vectors with human participants' ratings of interpretable features. In summary, we derive new insights into LM modal categorization using techniques from mechanistic interpretability, with the potential to inform our understanding of modal categorization in humans.

papers.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Channels in Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic channels in convolutional neural networks be identified and disentangled into monosemantic channels to improve interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an algorithm to identify and disentangle polysemantic channels in pre-trained CNNs into multiple channels, each activating for a single concept, without affecting predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool effectively identifies and disentangles γ-polysemantic channels in CNNs, enhancing mechanistic interpretability and feature visualization.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully disentangles polysemantic channels, as shown with channel #1660 for 'digital clock' and 'cauliflower' concepts, where disentangled channels mimic original activations for their respective concepts.
Quantitative analysis shows that for polysemantic channels, the first disentangled channel activates strongly for concept 1 (114% relative activation) and weakly for concept 2 (-9%), while the second shows the opposite pattern.
The residual channel has near-zero activation, indicating it captures minimal information beyond the disentangled concepts.
Feature visualizations (e.g., with MACO) for disentangled channels show more isolated concepts compared to the original polysemantic channel.
The approach is based on attribution methods and cosine similarity of average relevance vectors to identify polysemanticity.
papers.limitation:
Currently only applied to disentanglement of two concepts.
The formulation of polysemanticity is based on class labels, which may work better in later layers with more semantically meaningful concepts.
Relies on handpicked hyperparameters (τ, γ, p) for identification, which are application-specific.
future_direction: Extend the method to more than two concepts, e.g., through recursive application.
Explore the impact of hyperparameters and develop methods for setting them automatically.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability is concerned with analyzing individual components in a (convolutional) neural network (CNN) and how they form larger circuits representing decision mechanisms. These investigations are challenging since CNNs frequently learn polysemantic channels that encode distinct concepts, making them hard to interpret. To address this, we propose an algorithm to disentangle a specific kind of polysemantic channel into multiple channels, each responding to a single concept. Our approach restructures weights in a CNN, utilizing that different concepts within the same channel exhibit distinct activation patterns in the previous layer. By disentangling these polysemantic features, we enhance the interpretability of CNNs, ultimately improving explanatory techniques such as feature visualizations.

papers.title: Can Role Vectors Affect LLM Behaviour?
papers.research_question: Can we identify role vectors in the activation space that improve performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does ablating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces role vectors, a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this approach improves in-domain and cross-domain task performance more effectively than persona-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors can effectively steer LLM behavior and improve performance on objective tasks, providing a more direct and effective control mechanism than persona-based prompting.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can be identified and used to improve performance on domain-specific tasks, with in-domain improvements and unexpected cross-domain gains.
Ablating the role vectors degrades performance, indicating their causal role in the model's behavior.
The effect of role vectors is more consistent and substantial than traditional persona-based prompting.
The results support the linear representation hypothesis, showing that high-level concepts are linearly represented in the activation space.
The method generalizes across multiple models and domains, as shown by cross-dataset validation on MedQA.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving in-domain task performance while also yielding unexpected cross-domain gains. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: time2time: Causal Intervention in Hidden States to Simulate Rare Events in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do time series foundation models internalize semantic concepts like market regimes, and can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare events such as market crashes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation transplantation, a causal intervention method that provides evidence that time series foundation models learn high-level semantic concepts of real-world events, enabling steerable simulations for stress-testing.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides causal evidence that time series foundation models encode abstract, steerable market regime concepts, enabling deterministic control of forecasts and revealing a continuous severity axis in their latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Activation transplantation can deterministically steer forecasts by implanting the statistical signature of one event into another.
Models encode event severity as a continuous latent variable, with the activation vector norm correlating with shock magnitude.
The steerable representations are robust across different model architectures (decoder-only Toto and encoder-decoder Chronos).
A unified 'crash' concept emerges across layers, with early layers showing anti-correlation and later layers converging to a shared subspace.
The model's internal representation of a crash is not binary but continuous, allowing for graded interventions.
papers.limitation: The work is a foundational proof-of-concept and it remains to be investigated whether steerable semantic subspaces are universal beyond Transformers to other architectures like State Space Models or LSTMs.
future_direction: Investigate whether steerable semantic subspaces are universal across sequence models beyond Transformers, such as State Space Models and LSTMs.
Discover a broader semantic vocabulary within TSFMs, probing for concepts like earnings surprises in finance or seizure onsets in EEG data.
papers.abstract: While transformer-based foundation models excel at forecasting routine patterns, two questions remain: do they internalize semantic concepts such as market regimes, or merely fit curves? And can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare, high-stakes events such as market crashes? To investigate this, we introduce activation transplantation, a causal intervention that manipulates hidden states by imposing the statistical moments of one event (e.g., a historical crash) onto another (e.g., a calm period) during the forward pass. This procedure deterministically steers forecasts: injecting crash semantics induces downturn predictions, while injecting calm semantics suppresses crashes and restores stability. Beyond binary control, we find that models encode a graded notion of event severity, with the latent vector norm directly correlating with the magnitude of systemic shocks. Validated across two architecturally distinct TSFMs, Toto (decoder only) and Chronos (encoder-decoder), our results demonstrate that steerable, semantically grounded representations are a robust property of large time series transformers. Our findings provide evidence for a latent concept space that governs model predictions, shifting interpretability from post-hoc attribution to direct causal intervention, and enabling semantic "what-if" analysis for strategic stress-testing.

papers.title: Do Llamas understand the periodic table?
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the periodic table of elements, and what is the geometric structure of their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally develop structured geometric representations (a 3D spiral) of the periodic table in their hidden states, with knowledge encoded as continuous manifolds in middle layers that sharpen into categorical distinctions in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent symbolic scientific knowledge as coherent, geometry-aware manifolds that reflect the natural order of the physical world, which can inform interpretability and trust in LLMs for scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure in LLM hidden states aligns with the conceptual organization of the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous, overlapping attribute subspaces, while deeper layers sharpen decision boundaries and integrate linguistic context.
Linguistic structure increasingly shapes factual representations in later layers.
Strong linear associations between related attributes in middle layers enable indirect recall.
Regression probing shows continuous numerical features are effectively represented in intermediate layers, while classification probing shows later layers are better for fine-grained categorical decisions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to chemical elements in the periodic table; future studies could expand to other chemical structures and properties.
The hypothesis-driven validation of geometric structures may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Expand to other chemical structures and properties.
Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge.
papers.abstract: We observe a 3D spiral structure in the hidden states of LLMs that aligns with the conceptual structure of the periodic table.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: A Framework for Interpretability in Machine Learning for Medical Imaging
papers.research_question: Why does the need for interpretability in machine learning for medical imaging (MLMI) arise? What are the underlying elements of interpretability in MLMI? How can we formalize these into a framework for interpretability in MLMI?
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes interpretability needs in medical imaging by identifying five core elements (localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability) and proposes a framework to guide practitioners in designing and evaluating interpretable MLMI methods.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes interpretability in medical imaging through a framework based on five core elements, aiming to guide method design, improve real-world usage, and inspire future research.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability in MLMI can be decomposed into five core elements: localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability.
A framework is proposed that connects real-world medical imaging tasks and objectives to these interpretability elements and existing methods.
The framework provides a step-by-step guide for practitioners to approach interpretability in MLMI, from defining the problem to selecting appropriate methods.
Interpretability methods should be chosen based on the specific real-world objectives (e.g., troubleshooting, fairness, trust) and the intended users (e.g., clinicians, researchers).
Pixel-level tasks (e.g., segmentation, registration) have inherent interpretability due to their localizable and visually recognizable outputs.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability might induce or contribute to human biases such as automation bias (too much trust) or algorithmic aversion (too much distrust).
Low-dimensional projections of high-dimensional internal representations (e.g., 2D heatmaps) can give users a false sense of understanding.
Interpretability is not always necessary and can potentially hinder model performance or introduce new biases.
future_direction: Developing interpretability methods that address multiple elements simultaneously.
Creating benchmarks and evaluation metrics specifically for interpretability methods in MLMI.
Studying the impact of interpretability on clinical decision-making and outcomes.
Exploring the role of interpretability in the regulatory approval of MLMI systems.
papers.abstract: Interpretability for machine learning models in medical imaging (MLMI) is an important direction of research. However, there is a general sense of murkiness in what interpretability means. Why does the need for interpretability in MLMI arise? What goals does one actually seek to address when interpretability is needed? To answer these questions, we identify a need to formalize the goals and elements of interpretability in MLMI. By reasoning about real-world tasks and goals common in both medical image analysis and its intersection with machine learning, we identify five core elements of interpretability: localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability. From this, we arrive at a framework for interpretability in MLMI, which serves as a step-by-step guide to approaching interpretability in this context. Overall, this paper formalizes interpretability needs in the context of medical imaging, and our applied perspective clarifies concrete MLMI-specific goals and considerations in order to guide method design and improve real-world usage. Our goal is to provide practical and didactic information for model designers and practitioners, inspire developers of models in the medical imaging field to reason more deeply about what interpretability is achieving, and suggest future directions of interpretability research.

papers.title: Large Language Models Encode Semantics and Alignment in Linearly Separable Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models encode high-level semantic information in linearly separable representations across domains and alignment behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode high-level semantics and alignment behaviors in linearly separable representations, enabling effective latent-space guardrails for safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs organize high-level semantics and alignment in linearly separable subspaces, motivating geometry-aware tools for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic representations become increasingly linearly separable in deeper layers.
Linear separability persists even when domain-specific keywords are masked.
Instruction following (e.g., chain-of-thought) induces linearly separable representations.
Safety-aligned models show separable clusters for benign and harmful prompts.
A lightweight MLP guardrail on hidden states improves refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
future_direction: Adversarial perturbation studies for causal validation
Axis-orthogonality tests for linear representations
Further research on information distribution across architectures
papers.abstract: Understanding the latent space geometry of large language models (LLMs) is key to interpreting their behavior and improving alignment. Yet it remains unclear to what extent LLMs linearly organize representations related to semantic understanding. To explore this, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of hidden representations in 11 autoregressive models across six scientific topics. We find that high-level semantic information consistently resides in low-dimensional subspaces that form linearly separable representations across domains. This separability becomes more pronounced in deeper layers and under prompts that elicit structured reasoning or alignment behavior$\unicode{x2013}$even when surface content remains unchanged. These findings motivate geometry-aware tools that operate directly in latent space to detect and mitigate harmful and adversarial content. As a proof of concept, we train an MLP probe on final-layer hidden states as a lightweight latent-space guardrail. This approach substantially improves refusal rates on malicious queries and prompt injections that bypass both the model's built-in safety alignment and external token-level filters.

papers.title: Operationally meaningful representations of physical systems in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks to learn operationally meaningful representations of physical systems that separate parameters relevant for different experimental settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture that learns operationally meaningful representations of physical systems by imposing a communication efficiency criterion between agents, leading to disentangled parameters that correspond to physically relevant quantities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed architecture can learn operationally meaningful representations that separate physically relevant parameters, and it can be combined with reinforcement learning for interactive settings.
papers.key_findings:
The architecture can separate local parameters from interaction parameters in classical charged particle systems.
It can separate local qubit parameters from quantum correlation parameters in two-qubit systems.
The method can be combined with reinforcement learning to learn representations in interactive scenarios.
future_direction: Combining the method with reinforcement learning for more complex environments.
Exploring other operational criteria for representation learning.
papers.abstract: Abstract To make progress in science, we often build abstract representations of physical systems that meaningfully encode information about the systems. Such representations ignore redundant features and treat parameters such as velocity and position separately because they can be useful for making statements about different experimental settings. Here, we capture this notion by formally defining the concept of operationally meaningful representations. We present an autoencoder architecture with attention mechanism that can generate such representations and demonstrate it on examples involving both classical and quantum physics. For instance, our architecture finds a compact representation of an arbitrary two-qubit system that separates local parameters from parameters describing quantum correlations.

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we find meaningful directions (concept vectors) in activation space that correspond to distinct features, starting from polysemantic neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors that represent distinct features, allowing for fine-grained concept separation controlled by a distance threshold.
papers.conclusion: Exploring directions in activation space (concept vectors) instead of individual neurons can lead to finding coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into concept vectors that are linear combinations of neurons.
The concept vectors encode coherent, human-understandable features, as validated by human experiments.
The method can separate fine-grained concepts (e.g., underwater scenes vs. scuba divers) by adjusting a distance threshold.
The latent space representations have higher similarity with the discovered concept vectors than with the neuron directions.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the data used to generate clusters.
All experiments were performed on image data, which may limit generalizability to other data types.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data.
Looking at other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how models store representations by breaking down neural networks into interpretable units. However, the occurrence of polysemantic neurons, or neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features, makes interpreting individual neurons challenging. This has led to the search for meaningful vectors, known as concept vectors, in activation space instead of individual neurons. The main contribution of this paper is a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors encapsulating distinct features. Our method can search for fine-grained concepts according to the user’s desired level of concept separation. The analysis shows that polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons. Our evaluations show that the concept vectors found encode coherent, human-understandable features.

papers.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can we identify functionally important features in neural networks? The paper investigates whether standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) learn features that are functionally important for network performance and proposes a new training method to ensure the features are functionally important.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces end-to-end sparse dictionary learning, a method for training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that ensures the learned features are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted.
