Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: SourceNet: Interpretable Sim-to-Real Inference on Variable-Geometry Sensor Arrays for Earthquake Source Inversion
papers.research_question: How to infer high-dimensional physical states (earthquake source parameters) from sparse, ad-hoc sensor arrays, bridging the Sim-to-Real gap via physics-structured domain randomization.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SourceNet, a Transformer-based framework for earthquake source inversion that bridges the Sim-to-Real gap via Physics-Structured Domain Randomization (PSDR), and shows the model autonomously discovers optimal experimental design principles.
papers.conclusion: SourceNet bridges deep learning and rigorous physical inference on variable-geometry arrays, and demonstrates that interpretability can lead to discovery of physical strategies such as optimal experimental design.
papers.key_findings:
SourceNet achieves state-of-the-art precision on held-out real earthquake data, demonstrating effective Sim-to-Real transfer.
Physics-Structured Domain Randomization (PSDR) enables robust feature learning invariant to unmodeled environmental heterogeneity.
Self-attention is theoretically superior to pooling-based baselines (e.g., DeepSets) for wave physics, capturing relational dependencies.
Interpretability analysis reveals the model autonomously discovers geometric information bottlenecks and learns an attention policy that prioritizes sparse sensor placements, recovering principles of optimal experimental design.
The model uses full-waveform information, including scattered coda phases typically ignored by classical solvers.
papers.limitation: The framework assumes the simulation covers the physics of the real world, and out-of-distribution events (e.g., complex multi-fault ruptures) remain challenging.
future_direction: Extend the framework to model the full spatiotemporal evolution of fault slip using neural surrogates.
papers.abstract: Inferring high-dimensional physical states from sparse, ad-hoc sensor arrays is a fundamental challenge across AI for Science, yet standard architectures like CNNs and DeepSets struggle to capture the irregular geometries and relational physics inherent to domains like seismology. To address this, we propose SourceNet, a Transformer-based framework that bridges the profound Sim-to-Real gap via Physics-Structured Domain Randomization (PSDR), a protocol that randomizes governing physical dynamics to enforce invariance to unmodeled environmental heterogeneity. By pre-training on 100,000 synthetic events and fine-tuning on ~2,500 real-world events, SourceNet achieves state-of-the-art precision on held-out real data, demonstrating exceptional data efficiency and real-time capability compared to classical solvers. Beyond prediction, interpretability analysis reveals that the model shows scientific-agent-like features: it autonomously discovers geometric information bottlenecks and learns an attention policy that prioritizes sparse sensor placements, effectively recovering principles of optimal experimental design from data alone.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler's predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model's inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: Toward Knowledge Extraction in Classification of Volcano-Seismic Events: Visualizing Hidden States in Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we understand what and how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) model in the context of volcano-seismic event classification, and how can this knowledge be used to improve data interpretation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces visualization approaches to understand the hidden state dynamics of RNNs in volcano-seismic event classification, showing how neuron specialization varies with architecture and event type, and how this can be used for network pruning and active learning.
papers.conclusion: The visualization approaches help understand RNN internal mechanisms, and neuron specialization can be used for network pruning and active learning in volcano-seismic event classification.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM architectures exhibit lower neuronal activity and better specialization compared to Vanilla RNN.
Neurons specialize for specific events and frequency bands, which can be visualized through activation maps.
The degree of specialization allows for network pruning (removing less specialized neurons) without significant performance loss.
LSTM architectures are more stable and have higher susceptibility to changes in input compared to Vanilla RNN.
future_direction: Exploring the correlation between dropout and specialization of neurons.
Using neuron specialization for active learning and network sparsity.
papers.abstract: Understanding how deep hierarchical models build their knowledge is a key issue in the usage of artificial intelligence to interpret the reality behind data. Depending on the discipline and models used, such knowledge may be represented in ways that are more or less intelligible for humans, limiting further improvements on the performance of the existing models. In order to delve into the characterization and modeling of volcano-seismic signals, this article emphasizes the idea of deciphering what and how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) model, and how this knowledge can be used to improve data interpretation. The key to accomplishing these objectives is both analyzing the hidden state dynamics associated with their hidden units as well as pruning/trimming based on the specialization of neurons. In this article, we process, analyze, and visualize the hidden states activation maps of two RNN architectures when managing different types of volcano-seismic events. As a result, the class-dependent discriminative behavior of most active neurons is analyzed, thereby increasing the comprehension of the detection and classification tasks. A representative dataset from the deception island volcano (Antarctica), containing volcano-tectonic earthquakes, long period events, volcanic tremors, and hybrid events, is used to train the models. Experimental analysis shows how neural activity and its associated specialization skills change depending on the architecture chosen and the type of event analyzed.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Neural Basis Models for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we scale Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to large datasets while maintaining interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Neural Basis Models (NBM), a new subfamily of Generalized Additive Models that uses basis decomposition of shape functions to achieve scalability and interpretability on large datasets.
papers.conclusion: Neural Basis Models address scalability and performance issues of GAMs while preserving interpretability, and can be used as drop-in replacements for black-box deep neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
NBMs achieve state-of-the-art performance among GAMs, with 5x-50x fewer parameters and 4x-7x higher throughput than Neural Additive Models (NAM).
NBMs scale to high-dimensional sparse datasets where other GAMs fail, and are more stable in terms of shape function consistency across training runs.
Pairwise interactions via NB2M can match or exceed the performance of black-box models like MLPs on many datasets.
NBMs can be extended to model pairwise interactions with linear parameter growth, unlike quadratic growth in NA2Ms.
The number of basis functions needed is small (B=100 for NBM, B=200 for NB2M) and the model is not overly sensitive to this choice.
papers.limitation: The approach has limitations with respect to the number of features; beyond 10,000 dense or 1 million sparse features, feature selection is needed to scale further.
future_direction: Explore visual interpretability by applying NBMs directly to pixel space or learning visual features with lower order interactions.
Use more interpretable basis functions, such as polynomials, for higher order interactions.
Apply feature selection algorithms to scale to even larger numbers of features.
papers.abstract: Due to the widespread use of complex machine learning models in real-world applications, it is becoming critical to explain model predictions. However, these models are typically black-box deep neural networks, explained post-hoc via methods with known faithfulness limitations. Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) are an inherently interpretable class of models that address this limitation by learning a non-linear shape function for each feature separately, followed by a linear model on top. However, these models are typically difficult to train, require numerous parameters, and are difficult to scale. We propose an entirely new subfamily of GAMs that utilizes basis decomposition of shape functions. A small number of basis functions are shared among all features, and are learned jointly for a given task, thus making our model scale much better to large-scale data with high-dimensional features, especially when features are sparse. We propose an architecture denoted as the Neural Basis Model (NBM) which uses a single neural network to learn these bases. On a variety of tabular and image datasets, we demonstrate that for interpretable machine learning, NBMs are the state-of-the-art in accuracy, model size, and, throughput and can easily model all higher-order feature interactions. Source code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/nbm-spam.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: GINN-KAN: Interpretability pipelining with applications in Physics Informed Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we create an interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN to overcome their individual limitations and be effectively applied to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GINN-KAN, a novel interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN, and demonstrates its application to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), creating interpretable PINNs that outperform black-box networks.
papers.conclusion: GINN-KAN represents a significant step forward in developing interpretable neural networks, offering a promising balance between interpretability and performance, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing machine learning frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets.
GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform traditional PINNs with black-box networks on 15 different partial differential equations.
GINN struggles to learn non-Laurent polynomial (non-LP) equations, while KAN struggles to learn equations containing multiplicative terms.
GINN-KAN combines the strengths of both GINN and KAN, performing well on both LP and non-LP equations and on equations with multiplications.
GINN-KAN can be trained using backpropagation and integrated into existing machine learning pipelines with minimal adjustments.
papers.limitation: GINN-KAN is restricted to inputs with positive values, a limitation inherited from GINN.
future_direction: Explore more robust architectures that maintain interpretability while overcoming the positive input limitation.
Develop better regularization techniques to enable GINN-KAN to accurately discover concise ground truth equations.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful function approximators, yet their ``black-box" nature often renders them opaque and difficult to interpret. While many post-hoc explanation methods exist, they typically fail to capture the underlying reasoning processes of the networks. A truly interpretable neural network would be trained similarly to conventional models using techniques such as backpropagation, but additionally provide insights into the learned input-output relationships. In this work, we introduce the concept of interpretability pipelineing, to incorporate multiple interpretability techniques to outperform each individual technique. To this end, we first evaluate several architectures that promise such interpretability, with a particular focus on two recent models selected for their potential to incorporate interpretability into standard neural network architectures while still leveraging backpropagation: the Growing Interpretable Neural Network (GINN) and Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN). We analyze the limitations and strengths of each and introduce a novel interpretable neural network GINN-KAN that synthesizes the advantages of both models. When tested on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets, GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN. To highlight the capabilities and the generalizability of this approach, we position GINN-KAN as an alternative to conventional black-box networks in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). We expect this to have far-reaching implications in the application of deep learning pipelines in the natural sciences. Our experiments with this interpretable PINN on 15 different partial differential equations demonstrate that GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform PINNs with black-box networks in solving differential equations and surpass the capabilities of both GINN and KAN.

papers.title: The Cognitive Revolution in Interpretability: From Explaining Behavior to Interpreting Representations and Algorithms
papers.research_question: How can we understand, interpret, and explain the behavior of complex intelligent AI systems like large language models, and how can mechanistic interpretability be grounded in cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper grounds mechanistic interpretability in cognitive science, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes interpretation methods into semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a cognitive revolution in deep learning interpretability is underway, shifting from explaining behavior to interpreting representations and algorithms, and calls for a unified framework that integrates semantic and algorithmic interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods are ripe for a transition echoing the 'cognitive revolution' in psychology, shifting from pure behaviorism to studying internal representations and processing.
A taxonomy mirroring computational neuroscience distinguishes semantic interpretation (studying latent representations) and algorithmic interpretation (studying operations and algorithms).
Semantic interpretation methods include optimization and search, structural probing, causal probing, and dictionary learning, each with distinct assumptions and challenges.
Algorithmic interpretation focuses on circuit discovery, using interventions like knockouts and patching to understand the role of sub-networks in model behavior.
The paper discusses parallels and distinctions between approaches, analyzes strengths and weaknesses, and outlines challenges and the possibility of a unified framework.
future_direction: Unifying semantic and algorithmic interpretation under a common framework.
Addressing challenges in scalability, evaluation, and the Rashomon effect in causal analysis.
Developing automated and scalable methods for feature interpretation and evaluation in dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have long been understood as "black boxes": though we know their computation graphs and learned parameters, the knowledge encoded by these weights and functions they perform are not inherently interpretable. As such, from the early days of deep learning, there have been efforts to explain these models' behavior and understand them internally; and recently, mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a distinct research area studying the features and implicit algorithms learned by foundation models such as large language models. In this work, we aim to ground MI in the context of cognitive science, which has long struggled with analogous questions in studying and explaining the behavior of "black box" intelligent systems like the human brain. We leverage several important ideas and developments in the history of cognitive science to disentangle divergent objectives in MI and indicate a clear path forward. First, we argue that current methods are ripe to facilitate a transition in deep learning interpretation echoing the "cognitive revolution" in 20th-century psychology that shifted the study of human psychology from pure behaviorism toward mental representations and processing. Second, we propose a taxonomy mirroring key parallels in computational neuroscience to describe two broad categories of MI research, semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned and used) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations) to elucidate their divergent goals and objects of study. Finally, we elaborate the parallels and distinctions between various approaches in both categories, analyze the respective strengths and weaknesses of representative works, clarify underlying assumptions, outline key challenges, and discuss the possibility of unifying these modes of interpretation under a common framework.

papers.title: Towards mechanistic understanding in a data-driven weather model: internal activations reveal interpretable physical features
papers.research_question: Whether interpretable abstractions corresponding to physical features are present in the internal representations of data-driven physics models like GraphCast, and if these abstractions are physically consistent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable physical features from the internal activations of the data-driven weather model GraphCast, and that modifying these features leads to physically consistent changes in predictions, offering a window into the model's black-box behavior.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders applied to GraphCast extract highly interpretable physical features, and modifying these features allows probing of the model's internal abstractions, contributing to model trust and potential scientific insight.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features in GraphCast corresponding to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal/seasonal patterns, precipitation, geographical coding, and sea-ice extent.
Features like sea-ice extent are learned dynamically even though not present in the model's input or output.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are identified, reflecting potential architecture bias.
Sparse probing identifies single features that strongly predict tropical cyclones and atmospheric rivers.
Interventions that modify a tropical cyclone feature lead to interpretable and physically consistent changes in hurricane strength and evolution in the model's predictions.
papers.limitation:
The correlation between sea-ice features and actual ice extent is demonstrated, but a more rigorous causal analysis is needed for a complete account.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are spurious and potentially undesirable from an interpretability perspective.
ERA5 fields themselves are not in perfect hydrostatic balance, which affects the evaluation of physical consistency.
future_direction: Conduct more rigorous causal analysis of the discovered features.
Build mechanistic accounts for the interaction of features leading to model predictions.
Train specifically sparse models to have interpretable computations.
papers.abstract: Large data-driven physics models like DeepMind's weather model GraphCast have empirically succeeded in parameterizing time operators for complex dynamical systems with an accuracy reaching or in some cases exceeding that of traditional physics-based solvers. Unfortunately, how these data-driven models perform computations is largely unknown and whether their internal representations are interpretable or physically consistent is an open question. Here, we adapt tools from interpretability research in Large Language Models to analyze intermediate computational layers in GraphCast, leveraging sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable features in the neuron space of the model. We uncover distinct features on a wide range of length and time scales that correspond to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal and seasonal behavior, large-scale precipitation patterns, specific geographical coding, and sea-ice extent, among others. We further demonstrate how the precise abstraction of these features can be probed via interventions on the prediction steps of the model. As a case study, we sparsely modify a feature corresponding to tropical cyclones in GraphCast and observe interpretable and physically consistent modifications to evolving hurricanes. Such methods offer a window into the black-box behavior of data-driven physics models and are a step towards realizing their potential as trustworthy predictors and scientifically valuable tools for discovery.

papers.title: How Much of a Model Do We Need? Redundancy and Slimmability in Remote Sensing Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do remote sensing foundation models enter an overparameterized regime at smaller scales than computer vision models, and do they rely on redundant representations?
papers.core_contribution: Remote sensing foundation models exhibit high post-hoc slimmability, retaining over 71% relative accuracy at 1% compute due to redundant representations, contrasting sharply with computer vision models.
papers.conclusion: RS FMs enter an overparameterized regime at smaller scales than CV models, with redundant representations enabling high slimmability, making post-hoc slimming a practical tool for resource-constrained deployment.
papers.key_findings:
RS FMs maintain over 71% relative accuracy at 1% computational budget across all models and tasks, a sevenfold improvement over CV models.
Learned slimmable training improves MoCo-based models but not MAE-based models, with MoCo showing advantages at low scales.
Feature correlation analysis reveals distinct scaling strategies: DOFA shows organized to independent features, Prithvi shows U-shaped patterns, and TerraMind shows monotonic decrease.
Explained variance ratio indicates that RS FMs distribute task-relevant information with high redundancy, leading to robust slimmability.
Intermediate-scale deployment often achieves superior accuracy through implicit regularization, offering up to 12x speedups.
future_direction: Develop slimmable training techniques for MAE's reconstruction objective.
Investigate modality-specific compression tolerances.
Explore non-uniform slimming strategies.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models (FMs) in remote sensing (RS) are developed based on the paradigms established in computer vision (CV) and have shown promise for various Earth observation applications. However, the direct transfer of scaling assumptions from CV to RS has not been adequately examined. We hypothesize that RS FMs enter an overparameterized regime at substantially smaller scales than their CV counterparts, where increasing parameter count primarily induces redundant representations rather than qualitatively new abstractions. To test this hypothesis, we use post-hoc slimming, where we uniformly reduce the width of pretrained encoder, as a tool to measure representational redundancy across six state-of-the-art RS FMs on four downstream classification tasks. Our findings reveal a significant contrast with those in the CV domain: while a post-hoc slimmed masked autoencoder (MAE) trained on ImageNet retains less than 10% accuracy at 1% FLOPs, RS FMs maintain over 71% relative accuracy at the same budget. This sevenfold difference provides strong empirical support for our hypothesis. We further demonstrate that learned slimmable training can improve both Momentum Contrast (MoCo)- and MAE- based models. In addition, through the explained variance ratio and the feature correlation analysis, we provide mechanistic explanations showing that RS FMs distribute task-relevant information with high redundancy. Our findings establish post-hoc slimmability as both a practical deployment strategy for resource-constrained environments and a diagnostic tool that challenges the prevailing scaling paradigm in RS. Upon acceptance, we will publish all code.

papers.title: Using explainability to design physics-aware CNNs for solving subsurface inverse problems
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques be used to design physics-aware convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for solving subsurface inverse problems?
papers.core_contribution: A framework for using explainability techniques (Score-CAM and Deep SHAP) to iteratively select CNN hyperparameters (e.g., kernel size, network depth) to develop physics-aware models for subsurface imaging that maintain high predictive accuracy while improving descriptive accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that explainability methods (Score-CAM and Deep SHAP) can be used to iteratively tune CNN hyperparameters, leading to physics-aware models with high descriptive accuracy without compromising predictive accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Initial deep CNNs (Transpose Convolution and Dense networks) had good predictive accuracy but low descriptive accuracy, as they focused on non-physical, low-power regions in the input dispersion images.
Changing the kernel size from 3x3 to 3x1 in deep networks did not significantly change predictive accuracy but showed slightly better descriptive accuracy.
Reducing network depth (shallow networks) improved descriptive accuracy, with the shallow 3x1 kernel network focusing primarily on the physically meaningful high-power modal trend in the dispersion images.
The shallow 3x1 kernel CNN is recommended as it achieves high descriptive accuracy (making logical, physics-aware predictions) without a considerable loss in predictive accuracy.
papers.limitation: The shallow network recommended is sensitive to noisy inputs and may require additional denoising layers for field applications.
future_direction: Adding denoising layers to the shallow network for robustness to noisy field data.
Extending the framework to tune more hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: We present a novel method of using explainability techniques to design physics-aware neural networks. We demonstrate our approach by developing a convolutional neural network (CNN) for solving an inverse problem for shallow subsurface imaging. Although CNNs have gained popularity in recent years across many fields, the development of CNNs remains an art, as there are no clear guidelines regarding the selection of hyperparameters that will yield the best network. While optimization algorithms may be used to select hyperparameters automatically, these methods focus on developing networks with high predictive accuracy while disregarding model explainability (descriptive accuracy). However, the field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) addresses the absence of model explainability by providing tools that allow developers to evaluate the internal logic of neural networks. In this study, we use the explainability methods Score-CAM and Deep SHAP to select hyperparameters, such as kernel sizes and network depth, to develop a physics-aware CNN for shallow subsurface imaging. We begin with a relatively deep Encoder-Decoder network, which uses surface wave dispersion images as inputs and generates 2D shear wave velocity subsurface images as outputs. Through model explanations, we ultimately find that a shallow CNN using two convolutional layers with an atypical kernel size of 3x1 yields comparable predictive accuracy but with increased descriptive accuracy. We also show that explainability methods can be used to evaluate the network's complexity and decision-making. We believe this method can be used to develop neural networks with high predictive accuracy while also providing inherent explainability.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: Using Degeneracy in the Loss Landscape for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does degeneracy in neural network parameterizations obfuscate internal structure for mechanistic interpretability, and how can we remove these degeneracies to obtain more interpretable representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of degeneracy in neural network parameterizations as an obstacle to interpretability, characterizes three sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis, a technique to obtain a representation invariant to these degeneracies, which may lead to sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that degeneracy in neural network parameterizations hinders interpretability, identifies sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis to remove degeneracies, potentially yielding sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Neural network parameters can be degenerate due to linear dependence between activations in a layer, linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer, and ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints.
Modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and a metric for identifying modules is developed based on this argument.
The Interaction Basis is a tractable technique to obtain a representation invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.
Representations invariant to degeneracies are likely to have sparser interactions.
The effective parameter count, derived from the local learning coefficient, measures the number of computationally relevant parameters in the network.
papers.limitation: The derivation of the Interaction Basis relies on two simplifying assumptions of independence about the Hessian, which are strong assumptions.
future_direction: Investigate alternative techniques for finding a basis without the simplifying assumptions about the Hessian.
Determine how to choose an appropriate behavioral loss cutoff epsilon for finite data singular learning theory.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to reverse engineer the algorithms implemented by neural networks by studying their weights and activations. An obstacle to reverse engineering neural networks is that many of the parameters inside a network are not involved in the computation being implemented by the network. These degenerate parameters may obfuscate internal structure. Singular learning theory teaches us that neural network parameterizations are biased towards being more degenerate, and parameterizations with more degeneracy are likely to generalize further. We identify 3 ways that network parameters can be degenerate: linear dependence between activations in a layer; linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer; ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints. We also present a heuristic argument that modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and we develop a metric for identifying modules in a network that is based on this argument. We propose that if we can represent a neural network in a way that is invariant to reparameterizations that exploit the degeneracies, then this representation is likely to be more interpretable, and we provide some evidence that such a representation is likely to have sparser interactions. We introduce the Interaction Basis, a tractable technique to obtain a representation that is invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.

papers.title: Interpretability and Generalization Bounds for Learning Spatial Physics
papers.research_question: How does the function space of training data affect the generalization of machine learning models when learning linear differential equations, and can learned models be interpreted in terms of Green's functions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generalization in learning spatial physics depends critically on the function space of the training data, and introduces a cross-validation technique and a mechanistic interpretability lens based on extracting Green's functions from learned models.
papers.conclusion: Learning spatially dependent problems is limited by the underlying function space of the training data, and careful data selection and cross-validation are needed; different model classes exhibit opposing generalization behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Learned parameters in finite difference models converge with error depending on grid spacing and polynomial order of data.
Linear models only converge to a projection of the true operator onto the subspace of the training data, limiting out-of-distribution generalization.
Deep models and SciML models (DeepONet, Neural Operator) do not always generalize out-of-distribution.
Physics-informed losses (PINNs, PI-DeepONet) suffer from the same subspace limitation as black-box models.
Green's function operators can be extracted from black-box models when they generalize effectively across test domains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis requires a priori knowledge of how the dataset was constructed.
Real-world data collection has inherent limitations that may hinder discovering unknown physics.
future_direction: Develop new methods capable of discovering the underlying subspace of the data to compensate for limitations.
Use cross-set generalization as an evaluation benchmark for future differential equation learning techniques.
papers.abstract: While there are many applications of ML to scientific problems that look promising, visuals can be deceiving. Using numerical analysis techniques, we rigorously quantify the accuracy, convergence rates, and generalization bounds of certain ML models applied to linear differential equations for parameter discovery or solution finding. Beyond the quantity and discretization of data, we identify that the function space of the data is critical to the generalization of the model. A similar lack of generalization is empirically demonstrated for commonly used models, including physics-specific techniques. Counterintuitively, we find that different classes of models can exhibit opposing generalization behaviors. Based on our theoretical analysis, we also introduce a new mechanistic interpretability lens on scientific models whereby Green's function representations can be extracted from the weights of black-box models. Our results inform a new cross-validation technique for measuring generalization in physical systems, which can serve as a benchmark.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Unveiling the Mystery of Weight in Large Foundation Models: Gaussian Distribution Never Fades
papers.research_question: What are the distributional properties of weights in large foundation models, and how can these properties be leveraged to simplify model adaptation and editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that weights in large foundation models follow a Gaussian distribution and that transformation weights can be derived from Gaussian noise, leading to a method that improves adaptation and editing by adjusting the standard deviation of the noise and updating outliers.
papers.conclusion: The Gaussian distribution of weights is a fundamental property that can be leveraged to simplify adaptation and editing, and optimal weights are sparse with a Gaussian-like distribution.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained weights of LFMs predominantly follow a Gaussian distribution.
Transformation weights (∆W) can be derived from Gaussian noise and primarily increase the standard deviation of pre-trained weights.
The standard deviation of transformation weights grows with layer depth.
Optimal weights should exhibit zero-mean, symmetry, and sparsity, with sparse values following a truncated Gaussian distribution and a few outliers.
Adaptation and editing can be improved by adjusting Gaussian signals and outliers.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a pioneering exploration of the mechanisms underlying large foundation models' (LFMs) weights, aiming to simplify AI research. Through extensive observation and analysis on prevailing LFMs, we find that regardless of initialization strategies, their weights predominantly follow a Gaussian distribution, with occasional sharp, inverted T-shaped, or linear patterns. We further discover that the weights share the i.i.d. properties of Gaussian noise, and explore their direct relationship. We find that transformation weights can be derived from Gaussian noise, and they primarily serve to increase the standard deviation of pre-trained weights, with their standard deviation growing with layer depth. In other words, transformation weights broaden the acceptable deviation from the optimal weights, facilitating adaptation to downstream tasks. Building upon the above conclusions, we thoroughly discussed the nature of optimal weights, ultimately concluding that they should exhibit zero-mean, symmetry, and sparsity, with the sparse values being a truncated Gaussian distribution and a few outliers. Our experiments in LFM adaptation and editing demonstrate the effectiveness of these insights. We hope these findings can provide a foundational understanding to pave the way for future advancements in the LFM community.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: Convolutional neural network-based liquefaction prediction model and interpretability analysis
papers.research_question: How to establish an accurate liquefaction prediction model using convolutional neural networks and interpret the influence of input features using SHAP analysis.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a CNN-based liquefaction prediction model that integrates Borderline SMOTE for handling imbalanced data and uses SHAP for interpretability, achieving higher accuracy than traditional methods.
papers.conclusion: The CNN model provides accurate liquefaction predictions, and SHAP interpretability analysis confirms the model's rationality and reliability for engineering applications.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieved an accuracy of 92.58%, outperforming other machine learning models and the Chinese building code method.
SHAP analysis revealed that soil layers with corrected standard penetration blows below 15 have higher liquefaction probability, while those with cyclic stress ratios under 0.25 are less prone to liquefaction.
The influence patterns of factors align with existing knowledge, validating the model's reliability.
papers.abstract: Conventional methods for liquefaction discrimination are often semi-empirical, prone to human factors, with low success rates and balance. Moreover, current machine learning approaches lack ample sample support and have specific limitations. Through the integration of liquefaction datasets, 11 features were chosen: corrected standard penetration test blows, fines content, soil layer depth, groundwater table depth, total overburden stress, effective overburden stress, threshold acceleration, cyclic shear stress ratio, shear wave velocity, earthquake magnitude, and peak ground acceleration. A convolutional neural network (CNN) model was established. The Borderline SMOTE technique was introduced to address the issue of imbalanced datasets. The CNN model was compared against random forest, logistic regression, support vector machine, extreme gradient boosting models, and methods specified in Chinese codes. Furthermore, the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) algorithm was utilized to examine the influence trends of input features on the prediction outcomes. The results demonstrated that the CNN model attained an accuracy of 92.58%, outperforming all metrics of the four machine learning models and the method specified in Chinese codes. Examination of the SHAP results unveiled that soil layers with corrected standard penetration blows below 15 exhibited a higher liquefaction probability, whereas layers with cyclic stress ratios under 0.25 were less prone to liquefaction. The influence patterns of each factor align with current understanding, indicating the prediction model’s credibility and reliability.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns.
