We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Unboxing the Black Box: Mechanistic Interpretability for Algorithmic Understanding of Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified taxonomy of mechanistic interpretability approaches, situates MI within the broader XAI landscape, and surveys key techniques and literature in the field.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems and invites new researchers into the field.
papers.key_findings:
The field of mechanistic interpretability has grown rapidly since 2020.
MI faces challenges such as superposition, spurious correlations, scalability, and evaluation problems.
MI offers opportunities for debugging, data privacy, robustness, control, human-in-the-loop, and trustworthiness.
future_direction: The need for standardized evaluation techniques.
Scaling up MI techniques to larger models.
Applying MI in real-world domains like finance and medicine.
papers.abstract: The black box nature of deep neural networks poses a significant challenge for the deployment of transparent and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. With the growing presence of AI in society, it becomes increasingly important to develop methods that can explain and interpret the decisions made by these systems. To address this, mechanistic interpretability (MI) emerged as a promising and distinctive research program within the broader field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). MI is the process of studying the inner computations of neural networks and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It encompasses reverse engineering techniques aimed at uncovering the computational algorithms implemented by neural networks. In this article, we propose a unified taxonomy of MI approaches and provide a detailed analysis of key techniques, illustrated with concrete examples and pseudo-code. We contextualize MI within the broader interpretability landscape, comparing its goals, methods, and insights to other strands of XAI. Additionally, we trace the development of MI as a research area, highlighting its conceptual roots and the accelerating pace of recent work. We argue that MI holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems -- treating models not only as tools for solving tasks, but also as systems to be studied and understood. We hope to invite new researchers into the field of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Neural Networks as Physics-Consistent Surrogates: An \textit{Explainable AI} Validation Framework for Learning Constitutive Relations
papers.research_question: How can neural networks for constitutive modeling of solid materials be validated and interpreted to confirm they learn physically meaningful principles rather than merely curve-fitting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops and applies a Physics-Explainable AI (XAI) framework to validate that neural network surrogates for constitutive modeling learn underlying physical mechanisms (stiffness, history-dependence, temporal damping) rather than just curve-fitting.
papers.conclusion: The Physics-XAI framework successfully validates that neural constitutive models learn physically interpretable representations of stiffness, path dependence, and fractional-order memory, transforming them from black boxes into transparent, mechanically grounded glass boxes.
papers.key_findings:
For hyperelasticity, gradient-based attributions (Grad Input and Integrated Gradients) match the analytical tangent modulus, proving the network learned material stiffness.
For elastoplasticity, SHAP and PCA show the RNN internalizes path-dependent memory, with plastic strain identified as the dominant feature governing stress prediction.
For viscoelasticity, latent-space and wavelet analyses of GRU layers reveal a temporal hierarchy encoding instantaneous elastic response, intermediate relaxation, and long-term fractional memory.
The Physics-Aware Distillation (PAD) procedure extracts interpretable material constants (e.g., Mooney-Rivlin coefficients) from the trained neural networks.
Quantitative metrics (MSE, MAE, R2, attribution correlations) confirm high fidelity and physical consistency across all three material models.
papers.limitation: The work focuses on uniaxial settings and noise-free synthetic data.
future_direction: Extend to multiaxial loading, anisotropic materials, and experimental datasets.
Integrate XAI with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).
Incorporate uncertainty quantification and robustness analysis for verification and validation.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a Physics-\textit{Explainable AI} (XAI) framework to validate and interpret neural networks for the constitutive modeling of solid materials. The study bridges the gap between data-driven models and continuum mechanics by applying a suite of explainability methods to neural networks trained on three distinct material behaviors: hyperelasticity (\textit{Mooney-Rivlin}), elastoplasticity (\textit{Chaboche}), and viscoelasticity (\textit{Fractional Zener}). First, high-fidelity surrogate models, including dense feed-forward networks, LSTMs, and GRUs, are trained on synthetically generated data to accurately capture complex material responses. The core of the work then employs XAI techniques to "open the black box" and confirm that the networks learn physically meaningful principles. For hyperelasticity, gradient-based attributions (\textit{Grad Input} (GI)) successfully match the analytical tangent modulus, proving the network learned material stiffness. For elastoplasticity, \textit{SHapley Additive exPlanations} (SHAP) and \textit{Principal Component Analysis} (PCA) demonstrate the \textit{Recurrent Neural Network} (RNN) internalizes path-dependent memory, with SHAP identifying \textit{plastic strain} as the dominant feature governing the stress prediction. For viscoelasticity, latent-space and wavelet analyses of the \textit{Gated Recurrent Unit. } GRU layers reveal a clear temporal hierarchy, with different layers encoding instantaneous elastic response, intermediate relaxation, and long-term fractional memory. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the XAI framework can verify that the neural networks are not merely curve-fitting but are, in fact, learning the underlying physical mechanisms of stiffness, history-dependence, and temporal damping.

papers.title: Identification of state functions by physically-guided neural networks with physically-meaningful internal layers
papers.research_question: How to predict the input-output relation in a physical system while fulfilling physical constraints, and how to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Physically-Guided Neural Networks with Internal Variables (PGNNIV), a method that integrates physical constraints into neural networks to predict system behavior and infer internal state variables, showing improved convergence, data efficiency, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.conclusion: PGNNIV is a promising framework that combines the predictive power of neural networks with physical interpretability, and shows advantages over standard neural networks in terms of convergence, data needs, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.key_findings:
The method accelerates the training process.
It reduces the amount of data required for similar accuracy.
It filters noise in experimental data.
It provides improved extrapolation capacity.
It allows obtaining internal state variables without additional assumptions.
papers.limitation:
For deep neural models, large and varied data are needed.
Defining successful network topology and hyperparameters is complex and time-consuming.
Predictions may not be as accurate as using full prescribed mathematical models.
papers.abstract: Substitution of well-grounded theoretical models by data-driven predictions is not as simple in engineering and sciences as it is in social and economic fields. Scientific problems suffer most times from paucity of data, while they may involve a large number of variables and parameters that interact in complex and non-stationary ways, obeying certain physical laws. Moreover, a physically-based model is not only useful for making predictions, but to gain knowledge by the interpretation of its structure, parameters, and mathematical properties. The solution to these shortcomings seems to be the seamless blending of the tremendous predictive power of the data-driven approach with the scientific consistency and interpretability of physically-based models. We use here the concept of physically-constrained neural networks (PCNN) to predict the input-output relation in a physical system, while, at the same time fulfilling the physical constraints. With this goal, the internal hidden state variables of the system are associated with a set of internal neuron layers, whose values are constrained by known physical relations, as well as any additional knowledge on the system. Furthermore, when having enough data, it is possible to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system and, if parameterized, to predict the state parameters for a particular input-output relation. We show that this approach, besides getting physically-based predictions, accelerates the training process, reduces the amount of data required to get similar accuracy, filters partly the intrinsic noise in the experimental data and provides improved extrapolation capacity.

papers.title: TabPFN Through The Looking Glass: An interpretability study of TabPFN and its internal representations
papers.research_question: How does TabPFN, a tabular foundational model, process and transform input features? What information is encoded in its hidden representations and how do these representations evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that TabPFN encodes intermediate and final quantities of simple arithmetic tasks in its hidden representations in a linearly decodable manner, suggesting the model performs structured, hierarchical computation internally.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN implements systematic, hierarchical computation, with intermediate results linearly represented in the residual stream, moving towards more interpretable and trustworthy tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear regression coefficients can be linearly decoded from the model's hidden states within a single model fit, but not across different fits.
Intermediate arithmetic terms (e.g., a*b) are linearly decodable from middle-layer activations, indicating the model respects the order of operations.
The final answer can be decoded from hidden states earlier in the network (layer 5) than it is correctly projected to the output space via the logit lens (layer 8).
Input values and their linear combinations can be decoded from the activations of the answer token early in the model, suggesting a copying mechanism.
The model does not maintain a fixed, universal encoding of coefficients across different fits; representations are fit-specific.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple arithmetic (additive/multiplicative) toy expressions, unlike the highly complex, noisy functions found in real-world datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex, real-world functions.
Using mechanistic interpretability methods like activation patching to find the mechanisms through which the answer is computed.
Manipulating the function through steering vectors or vector ablation.
papers.abstract: Tabular foundational models are pre-trained models designed for a wide range of tabular data tasks. They have shown strong performance across domains, yet their internal representations and learned concepts remain poorly understood. This lack of interpretability makes it important to study how these models process and transform input features. In this work, we analyze the information encoded inside the model's hidden representations and examine how these representations evolve across layers. We run a set of probing experiments that test for the presence of linear regression coefficients, intermediate values from complex expressions, and the final answer in early layers. These experiments allow us to reason about the computations the model performs internally. Our results provide evidence that meaningful and structured information is stored inside the representations of tabular foundational models. We observe clear signals that correspond to both intermediate and final quantities involved in the model's prediction process. This gives insight into how the model refines its inputs and how the final output emerges. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the internal mechanics of tabular foundational models. They show that these models encode concrete and interpretable information, which moves us closer to making their decision processes more transparent and trustworthy.

papers.title: Universal Redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: What mechanisms enable TSFMs to construct effective zero-shot forecasts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds universal redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), shows that middle layers are highly redundant and models are robust to ablations, and introduces an intrinsic head-pruning strategy based on stable rank to identify heads responsible for context parroting and seasonality bias.
papers.conclusion: The study sheds light on universal properties of TSFMs, revealing redundancies and providing an intrinsic head-pruning strategy that identifies heads responsible for common failure modes.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers in TSFMs are highly redundant and can be ablated with minimal performance drop.
An intrinsic head pruning strategy based on the stable rank of query-key projection matrices effectively identifies important heads.
Specific attention heads are responsible for degenerate phenomena such as context parroting and seasonality bias.
TSFMs exhibit significant variation in sensitivity to MLP ablations across architectures, with encoder-decoder models being more resilient.
The first and last layers are most important for model performance.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is technically limited to encoder-decoder models with causal masking.
The intrinsic head pruning strategy cannot account for the data-dependent exponential tilt term in the attention mechanism.
future_direction: Investigating how architecture determines what the transformer loads onto MLPs versus attention heads.
papers.abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) leverage extensive pretraining to accurately predict unseen time series during inference, without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. Through large-scale evaluations on standard benchmarks, we find that leading transformer-based TSFMs exhibit redundant components in their intermediate layers. We introduce a set of tools for mechanistic interpretability of TSFMs, including ablations of specific components and direct logit attribution on the residual stream. Our findings are consistent across several leading TSFMs with diverse architectures, and across a diverse set of real-world and synthetic time-series datasets. We discover that all models in our study are robust to ablations of entire layers. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical framework framing transformers as kernel regressors, motivating a purely intrinsic strategy for ablating heads based on the stable rank of the per-head projection matrices. Using this approach, we uncover the specific heads responsible for degenerate phenomena widely observed in TSFMs, such as parroting of motifs from the context and seasonality bias. Our study sheds light on the universal properties of this emerging class of architectures for continuous-time sequence modeling.

papers.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory
papers.research_question: How can coding theory and eigenspectrum analysis provide insights into polysemanticity and improve interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a coding theory perspective to neural network interpretability, using eigenspectrum analysis of activation covariance and random projections to understand polysemanticity, redundancy, and the trade-off between capacity and robustness in network codes.
papers.conclusion: The eigenspectrum analysis and random projections offer a top-down perspective on neural network interpretability, advancing understanding of code structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks learn codes that balance capacity and redundancy, with eigenspectrum decay indicating the level of redundancy.
Dropout during training leads to faster eigenspectrum decay, more robust codes, and smoother random projections.
Random projections of hidden activations reveal the smoothness of the code, which is linked to eigenspectrum decay and can complement single-neuron interpretability methods.
In large language models, random projections provide explanatory power in layers where single-neuron methods perform poorly, suggesting complementary approaches.
The framework explains polysemanticity as an efficient encoding strategy and provides theoretical insights into optimal coding and error correction.
papers.limitation: Identifying the exact error-correcting code is beyond the scope of this paper.
future_direction: A systematic study of how eigenspectrum decay changes with network size.
Investigating the role of nonlinearities in the network code.
Further research into the underlying structure and behavior of deep learning models from a coding perspective.
papers.abstract: Despite substantial efforts, neural network interpretability remains an elusive goal, with previous research failing to provide succinct explanations of most single neurons' impact on the network output. This limitation is due to the polysemantic nature of most neurons, whereby a given neuron is involved in multiple unrelated network states, complicating the interpretation of that neuron. In this paper, we apply tools developed in neuroscience and information theory to propose both a novel practical approach to network interpretability and theoretical insights into polysemanticity and the density of codes. We infer levels of redundancy in the network's code by inspecting the eigenspectrum of the activation's covariance matrix. Furthermore, we show how random projections can reveal whether a network exhibits a smooth or non-differentiable code and hence how interpretable the code is. This same framework explains the advantages of polysemantic neurons to learning performance and explains trends found in recent results by Elhage et al.~(2022). Our approach advances the pursuit of interpretability in neural networks, providing insights into their underlying structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.

papers.title: Randomness and signal propagation in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs): A neural PDE perspective
papers.research_question: What are the implications of the random-like weight matrices in trained Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for signal propagation and stability, and how can they be understood through the lens of neural PDEs and random matrix theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that trained PINN weights reside in a high-entropy regime consistent with random matrix theory, and that signal propagation in such networks can be interpreted through neural PDEs, with stability governed by the numerical properties of the underlying discretization schemes.
papers.conclusion: The neural PDE framework provides a useful perspective for interpreting signal propagation in deep networks, and the stability properties of the underlying numerical schemes are reflected in the structure of the learned weight matrices.
papers.key_findings:
Trained PINN weight matrices exhibit statistical and spectral properties consistent with predictions from random matrix theory, preferring a high-entropy regime.
Random and structured weight matrices can be associated with specific discretizations of neural PDEs.
The numerical stability of these discretizations governs the stability of signal propagation through the network.
Explicit numerical schemes (like the standard sequential PINN architecture) can lead to unstable signal evolution, whereas implicit and higher-order schemes yield stable dynamics for the same underlying neural PDE.
The failure of a PINN to learn the inviscid Burgers' equation is linked to deviations from random matrix statistics and unstable signal propagation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to the one-dimensional Burgers' equation and a specific PINN architecture (8 hidden layers, 100 neurons).
The connection between PINNs and (generalized) path integral solutions of PDEs is speculative and requires future exploration.
future_direction: Explore precise technical details of the connection between PINNs and path integral solutions of PDEs.
Extend the analysis to more complex PDEs and network architectures.
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often exhibit weight matrices that appear statistically random after training, yet their implications for signal propagation and stability remain unsatisfactorily understood, let alone the interpretability. In this work, we analyze the spectral and statistical properties of trained PINN weights using viscous and inviscid variants of the one-dimensional Burgers' equation, and show that the learned weights reside in a high-entropy regime consistent with predictions from random matrix theory. To investigate the dynamical consequences of such weight structures, we study the evolution of signal features inside a network through the lens of neural partial differential equations (neural PDEs). We show that random and structured weight matrices can be associated with specific discretizations of neural PDEs, and that the numerical stability of these discretizations governs the stability of signal propagation through the network. In particular, explicit unstable schemes lead to degraded signal evolution, whereas stable implicit and higher-order schemes yield well-behaved dynamics for the same underlying neural PDE. Our results offer an explicit example of how numerical stability and network architecture shape signal propagation in deep networks, in relation to random matrix and neural PDE descriptions in PINNs.

papers.title: Stiffness: A New Perspective on Generalization in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How does the concept of stiffness, defined as the effect of a gradient step on one example on the loss of another, relate to generalization in neural networks? How does stiffness depend on class membership, input-space distance, training iteration, and learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of stiffness, defined as the effect of a gradient step on one example on the loss of another, and shows that stiffness is a useful diagnostic for generalization, revealing semantic hierarchies and the effect of learning rate on the learned function.
papers.conclusion: Stiffness provides a new perspective on generalization that is sensitive to semantic content and relates to the loss landscape, and it can be used to diagnose overfitting and the effects of learning rate.
papers.key_findings:
Stiffness is high within the same class and increases between classes as training progresses, but decreases with overfitting.
Stiffness reveals higher-order semantic groupings (super-classes and super-super-classes) in CIFAR-100 without explicit training on these groupings.
Stiffness decreases with increasing distance between data points in input space, leading to the concept of a dynamical critical length ξ.
Higher learning rates lead to smaller dynamical critical length ξ, meaning the learned function is more localized and easier to bend.
Stiffness can be used as a diagnostic for overfitting, as it decreases when overfitting occurs.
future_direction: Using stiffness in architecture search and meta-learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper we develop a new perspective on generalization of neural networks by proposing and investigating the concept of a neural network stiffness. We measure how stiff a network is by looking at how a small gradient step in the network's parameters on one example affects the loss on another example. Higher stiffness suggests that a network is learning features that generalize. In particular, we study how stiffness depends on 1) class membership, 2) distance between data points in the input space, 3) training iteration, and 4) learning rate. We present experiments on MNIST, FASHION MNIST, and CIFAR-10/100 using fully-connected and convolutional neural networks, as well as on a transformer-based NLP model. We demonstrate the connection between stiffness and generalization, and observe its dependence on learning rate. When training on CIFAR-100, the stiffness matrix exhibits a coarse-grained behavior indicative of the model's awareness of super-class membership. In addition, we measure how stiffness between two data points depends on their mutual input-space distance, and establish the concept of a dynamical critical length -- a distance below which a parameter update based on a data point influences its neighbors.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: TIME: A Transparent, Interpretable, Model-Adaptive and Explainable Neural Network for Dynamic Physical Processes
papers.research_question: Can we recover an invariant structure (PDE) from dense space-time observations, detect anomalies, and make the network interpretable and transparent?
papers.core_contribution: A low-weight, fully convolutional encoder-decoder network that learns interpretable representations of PDEs from space-time data, with transparency and explainability.
papers.conclusion: The TIME network is effective for learning PDE representations and provides interpretability and explainability, allowing modelers to verify the network's workings against their domain knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The network can learn PDE kernels that approximate differential operators.
Network design (depth and number of kernels) affects interpretability and accuracy.
The network is robust to scaling and can detect missing data as anomalies in activation maps.
A compact representation (appropriate depth and kernel count) performs best while maintaining interpretability.
High-weight representations are redundant and impact interpretability.
future_direction: Imbibe complicated processes with additional domain constraints.
papers.abstract: Partial Differential Equations are infinite dimensional encoded representations of physical processes. However, imbibing multiple observation data towards a coupled representation presents significant challenges. We present a fully convolutional architecture that captures the invariant structure of the domain to reconstruct the observable system. The proposed architecture is significantly low-weight compared to other networks for such problems. Our intent is to learn coupled dynamic processes interpreted as deviations from true kernels representing isolated processes for model-adaptivity. Experimental analysis shows that our architecture is robust and transparent in capturing process kernels and system anomalies. We also show that high weights representation is not only redundant but also impacts network interpretability. Our design is guided by domain knowledge, with isolated process representations serving as ground truths for verification. These allow us to identify redundant kernels and their manifestations in activation maps to guide better designs that are both interpretable and explainable unlike traditional deep-nets.

papers.title: Decoding Dark Matter: Specialized Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Rare Concepts in Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently capture rare, subdomain-specific concepts in foundation models using sparse autoencoders, without simply scaling the SAE width?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs) for capturing rare, subdomain-specific concepts in foundation models, and demonstrates their effectiveness in capturing tail concepts and improving bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: SSAEs provide a powerful new lens for interpreting foundation models in subdomains, effectively capturing rare concepts and offering practical utility in tasks such as bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
SSAEs capture a greater proportion of tail concepts than standard SAEs trained on general-purpose data.
Dense retrieval is an effective data selection strategy for training SSAEs, outperforming sparse retrieval (BM25).
Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization (TERM) improves concept recall in SAEs, especially for rare concepts, at the cost of some precision.
In a case study on the Bias in Bios dataset, SSAEs achieve a 12.5% increase in worst-group classification accuracy when used to remove spurious gender information.
TERM-trained SAEs exhibit stronger activations and lower entropy for tail concepts, making them suitable for rare concept detection.
papers.limitation:
SSAEs require a small seed concept dataset to begin the data selection process.
TERM prioritizes recall, sacrificing some control (precision) for broader concept coverage.
future_direction: Extending SSAEs to other domains and modalities
Applying SSAEs to real-world safety-critical systems
papers.abstract: Understanding and mitigating the potential risks associated with foundation models (FMs) hinges on developing effective interpretability methods. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for disentangling FM representations, but they struggle to capture rare, yet crucial concepts in the data. We introduce Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs), designed to illuminate these elusive dark matter features by focusing on specific subdomains. We present a practical recipe for training SSAEs, demonstrating the efficacy of dense retrieval for data selection and the benefits of Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization as a training objective to improve concept recall. Our evaluation of SSAEs on standard metrics, such as downstream perplexity and $L_0$ sparsity, show that they effectively capture subdomain tail concepts, exceeding the capabilities of general-purpose SAEs. We showcase the practical utility of SSAEs in a case study on the Bias in Bios dataset, where SSAEs achieve a 12.5\% increase in worst-group classification accuracy when applied to remove spurious gender information. SSAEs provide a powerful new lens for peering into the inner workings of FMs in subdomains.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: A simple probabilistic neural network for machine understanding
papers.research_question: What are the properties of learning machines with a fixed internal representation, derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, in unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM), a probabilistic neural network with a fixed internal representation derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, and shows that it has desirable properties like continuity, controllable compression, and ability to support functions beyond generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that learning machines with a fixed internal representation, such as the HFM, operate in a qualitatively different regime from traditional models like RBMs, with data-specific information stored in weights and potential for higher cognitive functions.
papers.key_findings:
The HFM is uniquely identified by the principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance when hidden units are binary.
The HFM exhibits a phase transition at a critical coupling parameter g, with a divergence in specific heat.
Training the HFM with an EM algorithm allows features to be learned sequentially, with low-order features remaining stable as new features are added.
The internal representation of the HFM is robust to changes in the coupling parameter and dataset size, and low-order features capture most of the relevant information.
The learning modality of HFM is qualitatively different from RBMs: in HFM, data-specific information is stored in the weights, while in RBMs it is transferred to the internal representation.
future_direction: Investigating whether a universal data-independent internal representation emerges spontaneously in deep layers of learning architectures.
Relating the findings to thermodynamic costs of learning.
Exploring the hypothesis that internal representations evolve with depth in hierarchical learning systems.
papers.abstract: We discuss probabilistic neural networks with a fixed internal representation as models for machine understanding. Here understanding is intended as mapping data to an already existing representation which encodes an {\em a priori} organisation of the feature space. We derive the internal representation by requiring that it satisfies the principles of maximal relevance and of maximal ignorance about how different features are combined. We show that, when hidden units are binary variables, these two principles identify a unique model -- the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) -- which is fully solvable and provides a natural interpretation in terms of features. We argue that learning machines with this architecture enjoy a number of interesting properties, like the continuity of the representation with respect to changes in parameters and data, the possibility to control the level of compression and the ability to support functions that go beyond generalisation. We explore the behaviour of the model with extensive numerical experiments and argue that models where the internal representation is fixed reproduce a learning modality which is qualitatively different from that of traditional models such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines.

papers.title: A Structured Dictionary Perspective on Implicit Neural Representations
papers.research_question: What is the expressive power of INRs? How does initialization affect their inductive bias?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a unified theoretical perspective on implicit neural representations (INRs), showing they are analogous to structured signal dictionaries with harmonics, and that their inductive bias is characterized by the neural tangent kernel (NTK), with meta-learning reshaping the NTK like dictionary learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzes the expressive power and inductive bias of INRs from a unified perspective, showing harmonic expansion and NTK characterization, and reveals that meta-learning modifies the NTK to increase efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
INRs have expressive power equivalent to structured signal dictionaries whose atoms are integer harmonics of the input mapping frequencies.
The frequency support of INRs grows exponentially with depth as each layer splits input into higher order harmonics.
INRs suffer from failure modes such as imperfect recovery and aliasing due to their harmonic expansion.
The inductive bias of INRs is captured by the ability of their empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) to encode target signals efficiently.
Meta-learning increases the encoding efficiency of the NTK by constructing a rich signal dictionary from combinations of meta-training tasks.
papers.limitation: Most practical results are performed using one or two-dimensional signals, and insights should be extensible to higher dimensions.
future_direction: Generalize Theorem 1 to input mappings beyond sinusoids or include normalization layers.
Study the effect of out-of-distribution data on the alignment with the NTK after meta-training.
Design methods to visualize the eigenfunctions of the NTK in higher dimensions.
papers.abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to classical discretized representations of signals. Nevertheless, despite their practical success, we still do not understand how INRs represent signals. We propose a novel unified perspective to theoretically analyse INRs. Leveraging results from harmonic analysis and deep learning theory, we show that most INR families are analogous to structured signal dictionaries whose atoms are integer harmonics of the set of initial mapping frequencies. This structure allows INRs to express signals with an exponentially increasing frequency support using a number of parameters that only grows linearly with depth. We also explore the inductive bias of INRs exploiting recent results about the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK). Specifically, we show that the eigenfunctions of the NTK can be seen as dictionary atoms whose inner product with the target signal determines the final performance of their reconstruction. In this regard, we reveal that meta-learning has a reshaping effect on the NTK analogous to dictionary learning, building dictionary atoms as a combination of the examples seen during meta-training. Our results permit to design and tune novel INR architectures, but can also be of interest for the wider deep learning theory community.

papers.title: Causal Convolutional Neural Networks as Finite Impulse Response Filters
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether Causal Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with quasi-linear activation functions, when applied to time-series data with multimodal frequency content, exhibit properties analogous to Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters and can be reduced to an equivalent single-layer filter.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Causal CNNs with quasi-linear activations and long convolutional kernels behave like FIR filters, and the entire network can be reduced to an equivalent single-layer FIR filter optimized via least-squares, providing interpretability for system identification tasks.
papers.conclusion: Causal CNNs with quasi-linear activations and long kernels can be interpreted as FIR filters, offering a bridge between black-box neural networks and physically interpretable models for system identification in structural dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Causal CNNs with long kernels and quasi-linear activations can approximate band-pass FIR filters when trained on spectrally sparse data.
A multi-layer CCNN can be combined into a single equivalent FIR filter that is optimal in the least-squares sense, whereas a single-layer CCNN fails to achieve comparable performance.
In supervised regression, the learned CCNN filters implicitly capture the modal properties (natural frequencies) of a multi-degree-of-freedom dynamical system.
In an unsupervised setting using a VAE with a CCNN decoder, the model can learn and separate the natural modes of the system without access to excitation data.
The method is validated on real-world bridge vibration data (Z24 benchmark), showing recovery of expected natural frequencies.
papers.limitation:
The tanh-activated CNN is effectively linear only when activations lie predominantly near zero, which is a condition for interpretability as an FIR filter.
In the unsupervised learning task on a 9-DOF system, only the first 4 natural modes were reliably recovered, as higher modes were suppressed in the raw system dynamics.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the behavior of Causal Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with quasi-linear activation functions when applied to time-series data characterized by multimodal frequency content. We demonstrate that, once trained, such networks exhibit properties analogous to Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters, particularly when the convolutional kernels are of extended length exceeding those typically employed in standard CNN architectures. Causal CNNs are shown to capture spectral features both implicitly and explicitly, offering enhanced interpretability for tasks involving dynamic systems. Leveraging the associative property of convolution, we further show that the entire network can be reduced to an equivalent single-layer filter resembling an FIR filter optimized via least-squares criteria. This equivalence yields new insights into the spectral learning behavior of CNNs trained on signals with sparse frequency content. The approach is validated on both simulated beam dynamics and real-world bridge vibration datasets, underlining its relevance for modeling and identifying physical systems governed by dynamic responses.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Mechanistic Neural Networks for Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks that explicitly learn and solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) as representations in a parallel and scalable way to enhance interpretability and efficiency in scientific machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Mechanistic Neural Networks, a novel neural network design that incorporates a Mechanistic Block to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, and a parallel, differentiable ODE solver (NeuRLP) for efficient and scalable training in scientific machine learning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic Neural Networks are a powerful and versatile approach for scientific machine learning, capable of discovering and modeling complex dynamical systems with high interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic Neural Networks can discover governing equations from data and outperform the SINDy method in some cases, including for nonlinear and rational function derivatives.
The NeuRLP solver is efficient, parallel, and allows for faster training and longer rollouts compared to traditional sequential ODE solvers like Runge-Kutta.
The method is versatile and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on a range of scientific ML tasks, including PDE solving, equation discovery, and dynamical systems modeling.
The NeuRLP solver can learn adaptive time steps, becoming finer in regions where the fit is poor.
The method can handle multiple independent trajectories and learn a single governing equation from them, improving generalization.
papers.limitation: The cumulative error of the NeuRLP solver can become large for equations where the coefficients c0/c2 and c1/c2 are large relative to the step size.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Mechanistic Neural Networks, a neural network design for machine learning applications in the sciences. It incorporates a new Mechanistic Block in standard architectures to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, revealing the underlying dynamics of data and enhancing interpretability and efficiency in data modeling. Central to our approach is a novel Relaxed Linear Programming Solver (NeuRLP) inspired by a technique that reduces solving linear ODEs to solving linear programs. This integrates well with neural networks and surpasses the limitations of traditional ODE solvers enabling scalable GPU parallel processing. Overall, Mechanistic Neural Networks demonstrate their versatility for scientific machine learning applications, adeptly managing tasks from equation discovery to dynamic systems modeling. We prove their comprehensive capabilities in analyzing and interpreting complex scientific data across various applications, showing significant performance against specialized state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Moirai-MoE: Empowering Time Series Foundation Models with Sparse Mixture of Experts
papers.research_question: How can time series foundation models achieve effective unified training by moving from human-imposed frequency-level specialization to automatic token-level specialization using sparse mixture of experts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MOIRAI-MOE, a time series foundation model that uses a single input/output projection layer and delegates pattern modeling to sparse mixture of experts, enabling automatic token-level specialization and improving forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: MOIRAI-MOE is an effective approach for time series foundation models, achieving token-level specialization and superior performance in forecasting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
MOIRAI-MOE outperforms existing foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) in both in-distribution and zero-shot forecasting.
The decoder-only training objective is more efficient than the masked encoder approach.
The proposed token clustering gating function outperforms linear projection gating variants.
Model analysis shows that MOIRAI-MOE produces frequency-invariant representations in deeper layers.
Expert allocation reflects time series periodicity patterns, indicating token-level specialization.
future_direction: Pruning underutilized experts for model compression
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models have demonstrated impressive performance as zero-shot forecasters. However, achieving effectively unified training on time series remains an open challenge. Existing approaches introduce some level of model specialization to account for the highly heterogeneous nature of time series data. For instance, Moirai pursues unified training by employing multiple input/output projection layers, each tailored to handle time series at a specific frequency. Similarly, TimesFM maintains a frequency embedding dictionary for this purpose. We identify two major drawbacks to this human-imposed frequency-level model specialization: (1) Frequency is not a reliable indicator of the underlying patterns in time series. For example, time series with different frequencies can display similar patterns, while those with the same frequency may exhibit varied patterns. (2) Non-stationarity is an inherent property of real-world time series, leading to varied distributions even within a short context window of a single time series. Frequency-level specialization is too coarse-grained to capture this level of diversity. To address these limitations, this paper introduces Moirai-MoE, using a single input/output projection layer while delegating the modeling of diverse time series patterns to the sparse mixture of experts (MoE) within Transformers. With these designs, Moirai-MoE reduces reliance on human-defined heuristics and enables automatic token-level specialization. Extensive experiments on 39 datasets demonstrate the superiority of Moirai-MoE over existing foundation models in both in-distribution and zero-shot scenarios. Furthermore, this study conducts comprehensive model analyses to explore the inner workings of time series MoE foundation models and provides valuable insights for future research.

papers.title: From Compass and Ruler to Convolution and Nonlinearity: On the Surprising Difficulty of Understanding a Simple CNN Solving a Simple Geometric Estimation Task
papers.research_question: What does a simple CNN learn when trained to estimate the radius of a centred pulse or disk, and why is understanding this surprisingly difficult?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the difficulty of understanding even simple CNNs and provides a full theoretical design of weights for a radius estimation task, highlighting the roles of invariance and nonlinear activation functions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals that invariance and the number of flat regions in activation functions are key concepts for understanding neural network expressiveness, providing insights for interpreting more complex models.
papers.key_findings:
A simple CNN with ReLU can estimate radius for positive polarity signals but fails for both polarities due to limited expressiveness.
Theoretical analysis allows designing all CNN weights, which match empirically learned weights.
Invariance to intensity differences is essential for correct estimation.
The shape of activation functions (e.g., number of plateaus) affects network expressiveness; Sigmoid with more plateaus can handle both polarities.
Adding more layers or channels can improve expressiveness but complicates analysis.
papers.limitation:
The network is underparametrised and not representative of complex real-world models.
The analysis assumes ideal conditions like clean data and continuum approximation.
future_direction: Investigating the impact of domain discretisation and radius quantisation.
Scaling the analysis to more complex problems and architectures.
Exploring the role of activation functions with more plateaus.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are omnipresent, but remain poorly understood. Their increasing complexity and use in critical systems raises the important challenge to full interpretability. We propose to address a simple well-posed learning problem: estimating the radius of a centred pulse in a one-dimensional signal or of a centred disk in two-dimensional images using a simple convolutional neural network. Surprisingly, understanding what trained networks have learned is difficult and, to some extent, counter-intuitive. However, an in-depth theoretical analysis in the one-dimensional case allows us to comprehend constraints due to the chosen architecture, the role of each filter and of the nonlinear activation function, and every single value taken by the weights of the model. Two fundamental concepts of neural networks arise: the importance of invariance and of the shape of the nonlinear activation functions.

papers.title: Local vs distributed representations: What is the right basis for interpretability?
papers.research_question: Are dictionary-based representations more interpretable than neuron-based representations for understanding convolutional neural networks, and how does the choice of representational basis affect model comparisons?
papers.core_contribution: Dictionary-based representations are consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations in CNNs, and model comparisons based solely on neuron-level analyses can be misleading due to differences in superposition.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary-based representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, and comparing models using only neuron-based representations can lead to misleading conclusions about their relative interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary-based representations were consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations across three psychophysics experiments, with the advantage increasing in deeper layers.
ResNet50 exhibits greater superposition (lower axis-alignment) than VGG16, which masks its higher interpretability in neuron-based comparisons.
ResNet50 is more interpretable than VGG16 when evaluated using dictionary-based representations, but this difference disappears when using neuron-based representations.
Dictionary elements are at least as decision-relevant as individual neurons, as measured by Gradient×Input importance.
papers.limitation:
The experimental protocol may be confounded by semantics, as participants could solve trials by simple semantic grouping rather than identifying visual patterns.
The study is limited to two CNN architectures (ResNet50 and VGG16).
future_direction: Further refinement of the experimental protocol to better mitigate semantic confounds.
Examination of the interpretability of dictionary elements recovered by applying dictionary learning to full layer activations.
Expanding the range of architectures to understand why certain models are inherently more interpretable than others.
papers.abstract: Much of the research on the interpretability of deep neural networks has focused on studying the visual features that maximally activate individual neurons. However, recent work has cast doubts on the usefulness of such local representations for understanding the behavior of deep neural networks because individual neurons tend to respond to multiple unrelated visual patterns, a phenomenon referred to as "superposition". A promising alternative to disentangle these complex patterns is learning sparsely distributed vector representations from entire network layers, as the resulting basis vectors seemingly encode single identifiable visual patterns consistently. Thus, one would expect the resulting code to align better with human perceivable visual patterns, but supporting evidence remains, at best, anecdotal. To fill this gap, we conducted three large-scale psychophysics experiments collected from a pool of 560 participants. Our findings provide (i) strong evidence that features obtained from sparse distributed representations are easier to interpret by human observers and (ii) that this effect is more pronounced in the deepest layers of a neural network. Complementary analyses also reveal that (iii) features derived from sparse distributed representations contribute more to the model's decision. Overall, our results highlight that distributed representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, underscoring a need for the field to move beyond the interpretation of local neural codes in favor of sparsely distributed ones.

papers.title: Interpreting intermediate convolutional layers of generative CNNs trained on waveforms
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize intermediate layers in generative CNNs trained on raw speech data to understand how acoustic properties and linguistic units are encoded?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a technique to interpret intermediate layers in generative CNNs trained on raw speech by averaging over feature maps after ReLU activation, which yields interpretable time-series data. It combines this with linear interpolation of the latent space to show causal relationships between latent variables and intermediate layer activations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed technique allows for detailed interpretation of how acoustic properties and linguistic units are encoded across the layers of generative CNNs trained on speech, revealing causal links between the latent space and intermediate representations.
papers.key_findings:
Averaging over feature maps after ReLU activation in transpose convolutional layers yields interpretable time-series data that can be acoustically analyzed (e.g., for F0, intensity, formants).
Different acoustic properties are encoded at different layers: intensity is encoded in earlier layers, F0 appears in later layers (Conv4), and formant structure is primarily encoded in the final output layer.
Linear interpolation of individual latent variables (e.g., corresponding to the presence of [s]) reveals a causal relationship between these variables and specific activations in intermediate layers.
The technique can be applied to study higher-level phonological processes like reduplication, showing how such patterns are encoded in the network.
The proposed method scales to deeper models, with similar encoding patterns observed in a 10-layer WaveGAN trained on LibriSpeech.
papers.limitation:
The models are trained on limited and curated data, and the technique is applied only to GAN-based models, not to more commonly used ASR/TTS models.
Formant structure is only encoded in the final layer of the 5-layer models, partly due to Nyquist frequency constraints in earlier layers.
future_direction: Apply the proposed technique to other CNN-based models used in ASR and TTS, such as wav2vec 2.0.
Apply the technique to Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) used in unsupervised speech technologies.
Use the technique as a diagnostic to improve CNN performance, e.g., by adding more layers to better encode higher-frequency properties like formants.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a technique to interpret and visualize intermediate layers in generative CNNs trained on raw speech data in an unsupervised manner. We argue that averaging over feature maps after ReLU activation in each transpose convolutional layer yields interpretable time-series data. This technique allows for acoustic analysis of intermediate layers that parallels the acoustic analysis of human speech data: we can extract F0, intensity, duration, formants, and other acoustic properties from intermediate layers in order to test where and how CNNs encode various types of information. We further combine this technique with linear interpolation of a model's latent space to show a causal relationship between individual variables in the latent space and activations in a model's intermediate convolutional layers. In particular, observing the causal effect between linear interpolation and the resulting changes in intermediate layers can reveal how individual latent variables get transformed into spikes in activation in intermediate layers. We train and probe internal representations of two models -- a bare WaveGAN architecture and a ciwGAN extension which forces the Generator to output informative data and results in the emergence of linguistically meaningful representations. Interpretation and visualization is performed for three basic acoustic properties of speech: periodic vibration (corresponding to vowels), aperiodic noise vibration (corresponding to fricatives), and silence (corresponding to stops). The proposal also allows testing of higher-level morphophonological alternations such as reduplication (copying). In short, using the proposed technique, we can analyze how linguistically meaningful units in speech get encoded in each convolutional layer of a generative neural network.

papers.title: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Echo State Networks applied to Earth System Variability
papers.research_question: How can Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to make them interpretable, and how does this apply to the detection of El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) can be applied to Echo State Networks (ESNs) to interpret their decisions, and shows that the leak rate in the reservoir is a crucial parameter controlling memory and performance.
papers.conclusion: LRP can be applied to ESNs to open the black-box, and ESNs are effective for image classification tasks like ENSO detection, with advantages in training speed and parameter efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
LRP can be successfully applied to ESNs, providing relevance maps that highlight important input regions for classification.
The leak rate in the reservoir determines the memory time scale; too high leak rate causes the model to forget early inputs and performance drops.
ESNs achieve competitive accuracy with fewer trainable parameters compared to MLP, reducing overfitting risks.
The model focuses on the Niño 3.4 region for ENSO detection, which is physically reasonable.
The model is robust to random permutation of input columns, indicating it does not rely on the zonal structure of the data.
future_direction: Apply further xAI techniques (backward optimization, sensitivity analysis, salience maps) to ESN models.
Use ESN models for time series prediction with LRP as an alternative to attention mechanisms.
Apply ESNs with LRP to unsolved problems in climate and ocean science.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are known to be powerful methods for many hard problems (e.g. image classification, speech recognition or time series prediction). However, these models tend to produce black-box results and are often difficult to interpret. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is a widely used technique to understand how ANN models come to their conclusion and to understand what a model has learned. Here, we focus on Echo State Networks (ESNs) as a certain type of recurrent neural networks, also known as reservoir computing. ESNs are easy to train and only require a small number of trainable parameters, but are still black-box models. We show how LRP can be applied to ESNs in order to open the black-box. We also show how ESNs can be used not only for time series prediction but also for image classification: Our ESN model serves as a detector for El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) from sea surface temperature anomalies. ENSO is actually a well-known problem and has been extensively discussed before. But here we use this simple problem to demonstrate how LRP can significantly enhance the explainablility of ESNs.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: On Privileged and Convergent Bases in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the significance of feature directions represented by individual neurons in neural networks, and do networks converge to a unique basis across different training runs?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks do not naturally converge to a unique basis, but freezing early layers can enforce basis convergence, and linear mode connectivity improvements with width are not due to increased basis correlation.
