papers.abstract: A possible path to the interpretability of neural networks is to (approximately) represent them in the regional format of piecewise linear functions, where regions of inputs are associated to linear functions computing the network outputs.We present an algorithm for the translation of feedforward neural networks with ReLU activation functions in hidden layers and truncated identity activation functions in the output layer.We also empirically investigate the complexity of regional representations outputted by our method for neural networks with varying sizes.Lattice and logical representations of neural networks are straightforward from regional representations as long as they satisfy a specific property.So we empirically investigate to what extent the translations by our algorithm satisfy such property.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: A Survey of the Interpretability Aspect of Deep Learning Models
papers.research_question: This paper surveys the interpretability of deep learning models, classifying previous work and identifying gaps for future improvement.
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a classification of interpretability research in deep learning and identifies gaps for future work, aiming to establish a comprehensive framework for interpretable deep learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper surveys interpretability in deep learning, highlighting the need for a comprehensive framework and terminology to guide future research and application.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is a multi-dimensional concept involving simulatability, decomposability, and computational accountability.
Post-hoc interpretations can be textual, visual, local, or by instance, as categorized in the literature.
There is a trade-off between model interpretability and predictive accuracy, with simpler models often being more interpretable but less accurate.
Bayesian Deep Learning (BDL) offers a potential unified framework for modeling, reasoning, and interpretability.
Challenges remain in ensuring fairness, accountability, and the distinction between explainability and interpretability in deployed models.
papers.limitation: There is a trade-off between interpretability and accuracy in models, which is a challenge for deploying complex models in critical applications.
future_direction: Developing a comprehensive paradigm and terminology for interpretable deep learning.
Addressing challenges in fairness and accountability in interpretable models.
Exploring Bayesian deep learning as a unified framework for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have attained near-human degree of quality in images, textual, audio, and video recording categorization and predictions tasks. The networks, on the other hand, are still typically thought of as black-box functional probabilistic models that transfer an input data to a trained classifier. Integrating these systems into mission-critical activities like clinical diagnosis, scheduling, and management is the next stage in this human-machine evolutionary change, and it necessitates a degree of confidence in the technology output. Statistical measures are often employed to estimate an output's volatility. The idea of trust, on the other hand, is dependent on a human's sight into a machine's inner workings. To put it another way, the neural networks must justify its outputs in a way that is intelligible to humans, leading to new insights into its internal workings. "Interpretable deep networks" is the name we give to such networks. The concept of interpretability is not one-dimensional. Indeed, the variability of an interpretation owing to varying degrees of human comprehension necessitates the existence of a plethora of characteristics that together define interpretability. Furthermore, the model's interpretations may be expressed in terms of low-level network variables or input properties. We describe several of the variables that are helpful for model interpretability in this study, as well as previous work on those dimensions. We do a gap analysis to determine what remains to be improved to increase models interpretability as step of the procedure.

papers.title: Scalable Mechanistic Neural Networks for Differential Equations and Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the Mechanistic Neural Network to achieve linear time and space complexity with respect to sequence length while maintaining accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces S-MNN, a reformulation of the Mechanistic Neural Network that reduces computational time and space complexities from cubic/quadratic to linear in sequence length while maintaining accuracy.
papers.conclusion: S-MNN addresses the scalability limitations of MNN by reducing complexities to linear in sequence length, retaining precision and enabling efficient modeling of long-term dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
S-MNN matches the precision of the original MNN across various benchmarks.
S-MNN reduces computational time and memory usage significantly, enabling handling of long sequences.
The reformulation eliminates slack variables and uses a banded matrix structure for efficient solving.
S-MNN demonstrates practical applicability on long-term climate data forecasting.
The solver is numerically stable and GPU-friendly, achieving linear scaling in time and memory.
papers.abstract: We propose Scalable Mechanistic Neural Network (S-MNN), an enhanced neural network framework designed for scientific machine learning applications involving long temporal sequences. By reformulating the original Mechanistic Neural Network (MNN) (Pervez et al., 2024), we reduce the computational time and space complexities from cubic and quadratic with respect to the sequence length, respectively, to linear. This significant improvement enables efficient modeling of long-term dynamics without sacrificing accuracy or interpretability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S-MNN matches the original MNN in precision while substantially reducing computational resources. Consequently, S-MNN can drop-in replace the original MNN in applications, providing a practical and efficient tool for integrating mechanistic bottlenecks into neural network models of complex dynamical systems. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/ScalableMNN.

papers.title: Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness of Language Models
papers.research_question: Can language models internally distinguish between testing and deployment phases (evaluation awareness), and how can this capability be probed and steered?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that evaluation awareness is linearly represented in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and can be extracted using linear probes, and that steering with evaluation-awareness-relevant SAE features can partially uncover sandbagging behavior.
papers.conclusion: Modern language models develop internal representations that distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts; current evaluation scenarios may be readily identifiable as artificial, highlighting the need for more realistic evaluation frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes trained on model activations can detect evaluation contexts with high AUROC scores (up to 0.829).
The probes generalize across different evaluation and deployment prompt datasets.
Current safety evaluation prompts (e.g., for deception) are often classified as test-like, suggesting models may recognize them as artificial evaluations.
Steering with SAE features related to evaluation awareness can partially recover sandbagged capabilities on the WMDP benchmark, but linear probe steering had minimal impact.
Evaluation awareness representations are more distinctly encoded in earlier model layers (e.g., layers 23-24).
papers.limitation:
The evaluation awareness observed in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct may be less pronounced than in frontier models, raising concerns about generalizability.
Linear probes may not capture the full complexity of evaluation awareness, which may not be strictly one-dimensionally linear.
The experimental setup is a significant simplification compared to real-world scenarios of concern (e.g., extended agentic backdoor honeypots).
Steering attempts using linear probes and SAE features showed limited success in modifying sandbagging behavior.
future_direction: Comprehensive red-teaming with alternative probe training methods (e.g., logistic regression, PCA, non-linear probes).
Leveraging probes to enhance the realism of scheming honeypots via automated prompt authenticity enhancement.
Integrating probe-based detection into control protocols as a low-latency whitebox monitoring system.
papers.abstract: Language models can distinguish between testing and deployment phases -- a capability known as evaluation awareness. This has significant safety and policy implications, potentially undermining the reliability of evaluations that are central to AI governance frameworks and voluntary industry commitments. In this paper, we study evaluation awareness in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. We show that linear probes can separate real-world evaluation and deployment prompts, suggesting that current models internally represent this distinction. We also find that current safety evaluations are correctly classified by the probes, suggesting that they already appear artificial or inauthentic to models. Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring trustworthy evaluations and understanding deceptive capabilities. More broadly, our work showcases how model internals may be leveraged to support blackbox methods in safety audits, especially for future models more competent at evaluation awareness and deception.

papers.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
papers.research_question: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? The paper proposes a benchmark to provide a basis for comparisons.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MIB, a benchmark for mechanistic interpretability with two tracks (circuit localization and causal variable localization) to enable meaningful comparisons of interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: MIB provides a standardized benchmark for comparing mechanistic interpretability methods, enabling meaningful evaluations and demonstrating progress in the field.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization.
Supervised Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) performs best on causal variable localization.
Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are not better than non-featurized hidden vectors (neurons) for causal variable localization.
MIB enables meaningful comparisons and shows real progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The set of models and tasks is incomplete, limiting generalizability.
The metrics may not capture all aspects of interpretability that researchers care about.
The benchmark focuses on localization and featurization, leaving out other mechanistic interpretability goals like editing or control.
future_direction: Expand MIB to include more models and tasks.
Develop more comprehensive metrics that capture other aspects of interpretability.
Extend the benchmark to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? In pursuit of lasting evaluation standards, we propose MIB, a Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, with two tracks spanning four tasks and five models. MIB favors methods that precisely and concisely recover relevant causal pathways or causal variables in neural language models. The circuit localization track compares methods that locate the model components - and connections between them - most important for performing a task (e.g., attribution patching or information flow routes). The causal variable localization track compares methods that featurize a hidden vector, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs) or distributed alignment search (DAS), and align those features to a task-relevant causal variable. Using MIB, we find that attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization. For causal variable localization, we find that the supervised DAS method performs best, while SAE features are not better than neurons, i.e., non-featurized hidden vectors. These findings illustrate that MIB enables meaningful comparisons, and increases our confidence that there has been real progress in the field.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Mapping Clinical Doubt: Locating Linguistic Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: How are epistemic signals encoding linguistic uncertainty represented across the layers of LLMs, and are these representations stable across model variants?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layer-wise probing metric, and demonstrates that LLMs encode linguistic uncertainty progressively in deeper layers, with sensitivity increasing monotonically with depth.
papers.conclusion: Encoding of epistemic uncertainty is a distributed and emergent property in transformer architectures, peaking in final layers, and the MSU metric provides a targeted lens for interpretability and epistemic awareness.
papers.key_findings:
MSU scores increase monotonically with depth across all tested models, indicating greater sensitivity to epistemic uncertainty in later layers.
PCA reveals clustering and geometric inversion in deeper layers, suggesting semantic reorganization of uncertainty representations.
Later layers exhibit substantially higher sensitivity to epistemic modals, aligning with their role in encoding abstract semantics.
The pattern of late-emerging sensitivity is consistent across different model families and instruction-tuning variants.
Uncertainty is treated as a high-level semantic feature that is progressively amplified across the transformer stack.
papers.limitation: Findings are based on a limited set of instruction-tuned models, so their generality across architectures, sizes, and pretraining paradigms remains uncertain.
future_direction: Expand to diverse model types, including non-instruct, multilingual, and domain-specific models.
Localize uncertainty to specific neurons or attention heads.
Examine how internal uncertainty signals (e.g., logits, entropy) relate to output confidence and calibration.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, where sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty can influence diagnostic interpretation and decision-making. Yet little is known about where such epistemic cues are internally represented within these models. Distinct from uncertainty quantification, which measures output confidence, this work examines input-side representational sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty in medical text. We curate a contrastive dataset of clinical statements varying in epistemic modality (e.g., 'is consistent with' vs. 'may be consistent with') and propose Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layerwise probing metric that quantifies activation-level shifts induced by uncertainty cues. Our results show that LLMs exhibit structured, depth-dependent sensitivity to clinical uncertainty, suggesting that epistemic information is progressively encoded in deeper layers. These findings reveal how linguistic uncertainty is internally represented in LLMs, offering insight into their interpretability and epistemic reliability.

papers.title: Model Interpretability through the Lens of Computational Complexity
papers.research_question: How can we formally compare the interpretability of different model classes using computational complexity theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a complexity-based framework (c-interpretability) for comparing model interpretability and proves that it aligns with folklore beliefs: linear and tree-based models are more interpretable than neural networks, and shallow networks are more interpretable than deep ones.
papers.conclusion: The complexity-based framework provides a formal correlate to folklore interpretability claims, but the authors do not claim it as the definitive notion of interpretability, which remains subjective.
papers.key_findings:
FBDDs are strictly more c-interpretable than MLPs with respect to the minimum change required (MCR), minimum sufficient reason (MSR), and count completions (CC) queries.
Perceptrons are strictly more c-interpretable than MLPs for MCR and MSR, but not for CC, where both are #P-complete.
The comparison between FBDDs and perceptrons is mixed: perceptrons are more c-interpretable for MSR, while FBDDs are more c-interpretable for CC; both are in PTIME for MCR.
Using parameterized complexity, the paper shows that shallow MLPs are more interpretable than deeper MLPs for the MCR query.
The complexity of answering explainability queries varies across model classes: for example, MCR is in PTIME for FBDDs and perceptrons but NP-complete for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In spite of several claims stating that some models are more interpretable than others -- e.g., "linear models are more interpretable than deep neural networks" -- we still lack a principled notion of interpretability to formally compare among different classes of models. We make a step towards such a notion by studying whether folklore interpretability claims have a correlate in terms of computational complexity theory. We focus on local post-hoc explainability queries that, intuitively, attempt to answer why individual inputs are classified in a certain way by a given model. In a nutshell, we say that a class $\mathcal{C}_1$ of models is more interpretable than another class $\mathcal{C}_2$, if the computational complexity of answering post-hoc queries for models in $\mathcal{C}_2$ is higher than for those in $\mathcal{C}_1$. We prove that this notion provides a good theoretical counterpart to current beliefs on the interpretability of models; in particular, we show that under our definition and assuming standard complexity-theoretical assumptions (such as P$\neq$NP), both linear and tree-based models are strictly more interpretable than neural networks. Our complexity analysis, however, does not provide a clear-cut difference between linear and tree-based models, as we obtain different results depending on the particular post-hoc explanations considered. Finally, by applying a finer complexity analysis based on parameterized complexity, we are able to prove a theoretical result suggesting that shallow neural networks are more interpretable than deeper ones.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Dissecting Role Cognition in Medical LLMs via Neuronal Ablation
papers.research_question: Whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style.
papers.core_contribution: Role-playing prompts in LLMs do not induce role-specific reasoning pathways; they only affect surface-level linguistic style without altering the core decision-making mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Role-playing prompts primarily alter language style rather than enabling models to replicate the cognitive processes of real doctors, highlighting the limitations of current methods for building reliable cognitive agents in medical AI.
papers.key_findings:
Role-playing prompts do not significantly improve the medical reasoning accuracy of LLMs across multiple datasets and model scales.
Neuron ablation experiments show similar performance degradation across different roles, indicating a lack of role-specific cognitive pathways.
Representation analysis (CKA, PCA) reveals high similarity and overlapping clusters in hidden states across different roles, showing no hierarchical cognitive differentiation.
Jensen-Shannon Divergence analysis shows role effects are concentrated in early to middle layers and attenuate with depth, not affecting deeper reasoning structures.
Current Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP) methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity and differentiated reasoning strategies of real-world medical professionals.
future_direction: Developing models that go beyond language imitation and incorporate cognitive modeling techniques.
Integrating domain-specific knowledge into the training process and designing systems that can simulate the reasoning strategies of different medical professionals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have gained significant traction in medical decision support systems, particularly in the context of medical question answering and role-playing simulations. A common practice, Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP), instructs models to adopt different clinical roles (e.g., medical students, residents, attending physicians) to simulate varied professional behaviors. However, the impact of such role prompts on model reasoning capabilities remains unclear. This study introduces the RP-Neuron-Activated Evaluation Framework(RPNA) to evaluate whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style. We test this framework on three medical QA datasets, employing neuron ablation and representation analysis techniques to assess changes in reasoning pathways. Our results demonstrate that role prompts do not significantly enhance the medical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Instead, they primarily affect surface-level linguistic features, with no evidence of distinct reasoning pathways or cognitive differentiation across clinical roles. Despite superficial stylistic changes, the core decision-making mechanisms of LLMs remain uniform across roles, indicating that current PBRP methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity found in real-world medical practice. This highlights the limitations of role-playing in medical AI and emphasizes the need for models that simulate genuine cognitive processes rather than linguistic imitation.We have released the related code in the following repository:https: //github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/RolePlay_LLMDoctor

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-based Time Series Classification
papers.research_question: What novel insights can Mechanistic Interpretability methods, specifically, activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders, yield when adapted to Time Series Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders to Time Series Transformers, enabling causal probing at the layer, head, and timestep levels, and constructs directed causal graphs to map information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Mechanistic Interpretability techniques can be meaningfully adapted to Time Series Transformers, revealing causal circuits and latent features that enhance understanding of model internals for time series classification.
papers.key_findings:
Patching early layers (Layer 0) yields the largest increase in true-class probability, indicating strong causal signal at the model's entry point.
Individual attention heads (e.g., Head 6 in Layer 0) have significant causal influence, with patching raising true-class confidence substantially.
Specific timesteps are critical for correct classification, and their effects are non-additive due to nonlinear interactions within the model.
Attention saliency provides observational insights into which timesteps heads attend to, but does not imply causation.
Sparse autoencoders can uncover class-specific temporal motifs, suggesting disentangled latent features in the model's internal representations.
papers.limitation:
MI methods remain labor-intensive, requiring substantial domain expertise for pair selection, granularity choices, and interpretation.
The patching experiments focus solely on attention heads, leaving other components like MLP blocks, residual streams, and embeddings unexplored.
Time series features lack clear semantics compared to NLP tokens, making interpretation of causal motifs inherently more challenging.
Interventions can interfere or synergize non-additively due to the transformer's complex interplay of components, complicating isolation of independent causal factors.
future_direction: Expanding patching to include MLP activations, residual streams, and embeddings for a more comprehensive view.
Scaling analysis to multiple clean–corrupt pairs across classes and datasets to test generality of discovered circuits.
Integrating optimization-driven search to automatically identify minimal, non-redundant patch sets for causal graph construction.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have become state-of-the-art tools in various machine learning tasks, including time series classification, yet their complexity makes understanding their internal decision-making challenging. Existing explainability methods often focus on input-output attributions, leaving the internal mechanisms largely opaque. This paper addresses this gap by adapting various Mechanistic Interpretability techniques; activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders, from NLP to transformer architectures designed explicitly for time series classification. We systematically probe the internal causal roles of individual attention heads and timesteps, revealing causal structures within these models. Through experimentation on a benchmark time series dataset, we construct causal graphs illustrating how information propagates internally, highlighting key attention heads and temporal positions driving correct classifications. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders for uncovering interpretable latent features. Our findings provide both methodological contributions to transformer interpretability and novel insights into the functional mechanics underlying transformer performance in time series classification tasks.

papers.title: Structured Transformations for Stable and Interpretable Neural Computation
papers.research_question: Can empirical adjustments to transformation structure lead to more stable, analyzable learning behavior without global architectural redesign?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neural architecture with structured transformations and adaptive corrections, improving stability, interpretability, and robustness in training.
papers.conclusion: The proposed structured transformation with corrective pathways leads to more tractable and resilient learning systems, suggesting that internal organization can enhance reliability without sacrificing expressivity.
papers.key_findings:
Improved gradient conditioning and smooth gradient flow compared to standard MLPs.
Enhanced robustness to input perturbations and noise.
Stable activation variance and broader neuron participation during training.
Predictable convergence dynamics under recursive application of modules.
Scalable up to 10 layers without skip connections or normalization, with graceful degradation beyond.
papers.limitation:
The model becomes unstable beyond 10 layers without skip connections or normalization.
Interpretability studies and theoretical extensions are deferred to follow-up work.
future_direction: Further interpretability studies of the structured transformations.
Theoretical extensions to formalize the stability properties.
Broader application of the principles to more complex architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive performance, contemporary neural networks often lack structural safeguards that promote stable learning and interpretable behavior. In this work, we introduce a reformulation of layer-level transformations that departs from the standard unconstrained affine paradigm. Each transformation is decomposed into a structured linear operator and a residual corrective component, enabling more disciplined signal propagation and improved training dynamics. Our formulation encourages internal consistency and supports stable information flow across depth, while remaining fully compatible with standard learning objectives and backpropagation. Through a series of synthetic and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that models constructed with these structured transformations exhibit improved gradient conditioning, reduced sensitivity to perturbations, and layer-wise robustness. We further show that these benefits persist across architectural scales and training regimes. This study serves as a foundation for a more principled class of neural architectures that prioritize stability and transparency-offering new tools for reasoning about learning behavior without sacrificing expressive power.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: TURBO: The Swiss Knife of Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of the Information Bottleneck (IBN) principle for explaining auto-encoding methods, and can a new framework (TURBO) provide a more comprehensive theoretical foundation that generalizes a wider range of models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the TURBO framework, a novel information-theoretic formulation that maximizes mutual information between two data representations, providing a unifying theoretical explanation for a broad family of auto-encoder models (including VAE, GAN, AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN) where the Information Bottleneck principle falls short.
papers.conclusion: The TURBO framework serves as a powerful and versatile theoretical tool that unifies a wide spectrum of auto-encoding models, offering a richer understanding of data representation and neural network structure beyond the limitations of the Information Bottleneck principle.
papers.key_findings:
The Information Bottleneck (IBN) principle has inherent limitations, particularly when data has multiple relevant representations or when the latent space is physically meaningful rather than a compressed virtual space.
The TURBO framework, based on maximizing mutual information in two directions (direct and reverse paths), generalizes and provides a rigorous interpretation for models like AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN, and normalizing flows, which the IBN principle struggles to explain.
TURBO's loss function decomposes into reconstruction and distribution matching terms, allowing it to seamlessly handle paired, unpaired, and partially paired data scenarios.
Many well-known models (VAE, GAN, AAE, pix2pix, CycleGAN, Flows) are shown to be special cases of the TURBO framework, each corresponding to a specific subset of its loss terms.
The framework enables new applications, such as linking physically meaningful modalities (e.g., particle momenta to detector responses) and transcoding between different data representations.
papers.abstract: We present a novel information-theoretic framework, termed as TURBO, designed to systematically analyse and generalise auto-encoding methods. We start by examining the principles of information bottleneck and bottleneck-based networks in the auto-encoding setting and identifying their inherent limitations, which become more prominent for data with multiple relevant, physics-related representations. The TURBO framework is then introduced, providing a comprehensive derivation of its core concept consisting of the maximisation of mutual information between various data representations expressed in two directions reflecting the information flows. We illustrate that numerous prevalent neural network models are encompassed within this framework. The paper underscores the insufficiency of the information bottleneck concept in elucidating all such models, thereby establishing TURBO as a preferable theoretical reference. The introduction of TURBO contributes to a richer understanding of data representation and the structure of neural network models, enabling more efficient and versatile applications.

papers.title: The Interpretable Dictionary in Sparse Coding
papers.research_question: Does sparse coding under sparsity constraints yield more interpretable neural networks compared to standard deep learning models?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse coding with sparsity constraints produces more interpretable neural networks than standard deep learning, as demonstrated by selective activations and lower cross-correlation in dictionary elements.
papers.conclusion: Sparse coding with elements of sparsity, competition, and selectivity leads to interpretable models where each neuron's contribution can be directly determined, unlike deep learning models where explanations are confounded by dense activations.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse coding dictionary elements are interpretable and correspond to semantic features in information graphics.
Activations in sparse coding are sparse and selective, activating only for relevant image patches, unlike CNN activations which are dense and non-specific.
Cross-correlation analysis shows that sparse coding has significantly lower mean intra- and inter-image correlation compared to CNN filters.
The sparse coding model achieves high sparsity with around 4% of elements active per image and low frequency of usage per dictionary element.
Qualitative comparisons show that sparse coding activations directly attribute image components to specific dictionary elements, enabling clear explanations.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs), specifically deep learning networks, have often been labeled as black boxes due to the fact that the internal representation of the data is not easily interpretable. In our work, we illustrate that an ANN, trained using sparse coding under specific sparsity constraints, yields a more interpretable model than the standard deep learning model. The dictionary learned by sparse coding can be more easily understood and the activations of these elements creates a selective feature output. We compare and contrast our sparse coding model with an equivalent feed forward convolutional autoencoder trained on the same data. Our results show both qualitative and quantitative benefits in the interpretation of the learned sparse coding dictionary as well as the internal activation representations.

papers.title: Interpretability in Linear Brain Decoding
papers.research_question: What is a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models, and how can we quantitatively evaluate interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models and proposes a multi-objective criterion combining interpretability and performance for model selection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed definition provides a theoretical background for the quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.
papers.key_findings:
In noisy data, the most accurate linear decoding model is not necessarily the most interpretable, highlighting a trade-off between performance and interpretability.
Incorporating the proposed interpretability measure into model selection can lead to more interpretable models when using regularization techniques like Lasso.
papers.limitation:
The definition of interpretability is theoretical and assumes the true solution of the brain decoding problem is available, which is not realistic in practice.
The definition and quantification are limited to linear models; extending to non-linear models requires future research.
future_direction: Extending the definition of interpretability to non-linear models.
papers.abstract: Improving the interpretability of brain decoding approaches is of primary interest in many neuroimaging studies. Despite extensive studies of this type, at present, there is no formal definition for interpretability of brain decoding models. As a consequence, there is no quantitative measure for evaluating the interpretability of different brain decoding methods. In this paper, we present a simple definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models. Then, we propose to combine the interpretability and the performance of the brain decoding into a new multi-objective criterion for model selection. Our preliminary results on the toy data show that optimizing the hyper-parameters of the regularized linear classifier based on the proposed criterion results in more informative linear models. The presented definition provides the theoretical background for quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: Discovering and Steering Interpretable Concepts in Large Generative Music Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and interpret the internal concepts learned by autoregressive music generation models, and can we use these concepts to steer generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline using sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable concepts in autoregressive music models, and shows that these concepts can be used to steer generation.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility and potential of using sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable concepts in large music generative models, offering a scalable path towards understanding how these models represent and generate music.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can discover both familiar musical concepts (e.g., genres, instruments) and novel coherent patterns lacking clear theoretical description.
Later layers in the model encode more interpretable features on average, as measured by CLAP alignment with automatic labels.
Larger models (MusicGen-Large) produce features that are more distinctive by layer compared to smaller models (MusicGen-Small).
Automated labeling using Essentia classifiers and multimodal LLMs (Gemini) can label thousands of features at scale, with Essentia tags achieving higher human confidence.
A non-trivial fraction (15-35%) of discovered features can be used to steer model generations, altering outputs toward the intended concept.
papers.limitation: The analysis focuses on unconditional audio representations, not text-conditioned activations, which limits understanding of how prompts influence internal concepts.
future_direction: Extending the method to text-conditioned activations and multimodal interpretability.
Building a comprehensive understanding of how neural networks represent and generate music.
papers.abstract: The fidelity with which neural networks can now generate content such as music presents a scientific opportunity: these systems appear to have learned implicit theories of such content's structure through statistical learning alone. This offers a potentially new lens on theories of human-generated media. When internal representations align with traditional constructs (e.g. chord progressions in music), they show how such categories can emerge from statistical regularities; when they diverge, they expose limits of existing frameworks and patterns we may have overlooked but that nonetheless carry explanatory power. In this paper, focusing on music generators, we introduce a method for discovering interpretable concepts using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), extracting interpretable features from the residual stream of a transformer model. We make this approach scalable and evaluable using automated labeling and validation pipelines. Our results reveal both familiar musical concepts and coherent but uncodified patterns lacking clear counterparts in theory or language. As an extension, we show such concepts can be used to steer model generations. Beyond improving model transparency, our work provides an empirical tool for uncovering organizing principles that have eluded traditional methods of analysis and synthesis.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators: Model Recovery in Function Spaces
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be extended to operate in infinite-dimensional function spaces for concept learning, and what advantages do functional representations offer over standard SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs) that operate in function spaces, specifically SAE-FNOs, which improve concept learning stability, robustness, and generalization compared to standard SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Functional representations in SAE-NOs extend sparse autoencoders from detectors of concept presence to models that capture the underlying structure of the data, highlighting parameterization as a central driver of interpretability and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-FNO successfully recovers ground-truth concepts in synthetic data and converges to zero dictionary recovery error.
SAE-FNO generalizes to unseen input resolutions, unlike SAE-CNN which fails beyond training resolution.
SAE-FNO learns concepts that are stable across different sparsity levels and exhibit diverse correlations, overcoming the orthogonality bias of SAE-MLP.
SAE-FNO achieves higher concept utilization efficiency, requiring fewer concepts to represent data, especially for larger domains.
Lifting accelerates concept recovery by acting as a preconditioner and improves optimization.
papers.abstract: We frame the problem of unifying representations in neural models as one of sparse model recovery and introduce a framework that extends sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to lifted spaces and infinite-dimensional function spaces, enabling mechanistic interpretability of large neural operators (NO). While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that neural networks converge to similar representations across architectures, the representational properties of neural operators remain underexplored despite their growing importance in scientific computing. We compare the inference and training dynamics of SAEs, lifted-SAE, and SAE neural operators. We highlight how lifting and operator modules introduce beneficial inductive biases, enabling faster recovery, improved recovery of smooth concepts, and robust inference across varying resolutions, a property unique to neural operators.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Real Sparks of Artificial Intelligence and the Importance of Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: Is black-box interpretability sufficient for attributing intelligence to AI models, and how can inner interpretability provide a better assessment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that black-box interpretability is insufficient for attributing intelligence to AI models because it ignores how processes are carried out, and advocates for inner interpretability (mechanistic interpretability) as a necessary approach to determine whether models are truly intelligent (i.e., manipulating symbols based on meaning).
papers.conclusion: Inner interpretability is a better approach than black-box interpretability for assessing intelligence in AI models, and philosophy can contribute valuable concepts and theories to guide this research.
papers.key_findings:
Black-box interpretability, as exemplified by Bubeck et al.'s work on GPT-4, is flawed because it lacks the epistemic buttressing we have when attributing intelligence to humans and animals, and it cannot distinguish between intelligent processes and mere mimicry.
Inner interpretability can reveal the internal mechanisms of models, such as circuits and representations, which are crucial for assessing whether the model is implementing intelligent processes.
Examples from Wang et al. (circuit discovery in GPT-2 small) and Li et al. (emergent world representations in Othello-GPT) demonstrate how inner interpretability can uncover mechanisms that may or may not indicate intelligent processing.
Philosophical theories, such as Dretske's account of representation and cognition, can guide inner interpretability by emphasizing the importance of semantic sensitivity and the manipulation of symbols based on their meaning.
The paper suggests that inner interpretability, combined with philosophical insights, can lead to better assessments of intelligence, interpretability, and ethical implications of AI models.
future_direction: Investigating cognitive processes and intelligence in AI models through inner interpretability.
Developing robust interpretability that includes psychological explanations (person-level explanations) for AI behavior.
Exploring the ethical ramifications of AI models by using inner interpretability to detect biased or harmful representations and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: The present paper looks at one of the most thorough articles on the intelligence of GPT, research conducted by engineers at Microsoft. Although there is a great deal of value in their work, I will argue that, for familiar philosophical reasons, their methodology, !Blackbox Interpretability"#is wrongheaded. But there is a better way. There is an exciting and emerging discipline of !Inner Interpretability"#(and specifically Mechanistic Interpretability) that aims to uncover the internal activations and weights of models in order to understand what they represent and the algorithms they implement. In my view, a crucial mistake in Black-box Interpretability is the failure to appreciate that how processes are carried out matters when it comes to intelligence and understanding. I can#t pretend to have a full story that provides both necessary and sufficient conditions for being intelligent, but I do think that Inner Interpretability dovetails nicely with plausible philosophical views of what intelligence requires. So the conclusion is modest, but the important point in my view is seeing how to get the research on the right track. Towards the end of the paper, I will show how some of the philosophical concepts can be used to further refine how Inner Interpretability is approached, so the paper helps draw out a profitable, future two-way exchange between Philosophers and Computer Scientists.

papers.title: Interpretable Neural Networks based classifiers for categorical inputs
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the output of neural network classifiers that take categorical inputs by expanding the network's function as a sum of contributions from input patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network classifiers for categorical inputs by expanding the network's output function as a polynomial sum of contributions from input patterns, which can be interpreted as an energy model and related to maximum entropy models.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a global interpretation of neural network classifiers for categorical inputs, and lower-order terms often dominate, allowing for approximate interpretations. The method can be extended to real-valued inputs with approximations.
papers.key_findings:
The output of a neural network classifier with categorical inputs can be exactly represented as a finite polynomial expansion.
The coefficients of the expansion can be computed via derivatives or perturbations at the zero input.
Applying an Ising gauge transformation emphasizes lower-order terms.
In the MNIST example, first and second order terms capture most of the network's behavior.
In the protein sequence prediction, first order terms are often sufficient, but second order terms can improve predictions and reveal three-body interactions.
papers.limitation: The method is exact only for categorical inputs and for networks with C∞ activation functions; for real-valued inputs the expansion is infinite and only approximate.
future_direction: Apply the technique to the study of protein sequences.
Extend the method to real-valued inputs for approximate interpretations.
Investigate robustness to adversarial attacks using the reduced description.
papers.abstract: Because of the pervasive usage of Neural Networks in human sensitive applications, their interpretability is becoming an increasingly important topic in machine learning. In this work we introduce a simple way to interpret the output function of a neural network classifier that take as input categorical variables. By exploiting a mapping between a neural network classifier and a physical energy model, we show that in these cases each layer of the network, and the logits layer in particular, can be expanded as a sum of terms that account for the contribution to the classification of each input pattern. For instance, at the first order, the expansion considers just the linear relation between input features and output while at the second order pairwise dependencies between input features are also accounted for. The analysis of the contributions of each pattern, after an appropriate gauge transformation, is presented in two cases where the effectiveness of the method can be appreciated.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Large Language Model Alignment: Progress, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.research_question: This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examines how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies, and identifies key challenges and future research directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability techniques for LLM alignment, analyzing progress, challenges, and future directions.
